Name three countries you'd like to visit, each with the right little word in front.
tutorPrompt: Be my A1 French tutor for countries and nationalities. Drill three things. ① Country names with their articles — la France, l'Italie, l'Espagne, l'Inde, la Chine, le Japon, le Portugal, le Maroc, le Canada, le Brésil, les États-Unis, les Pays-Bas — and make me say whether each is feminine, masculine or plural. ② The nationality endings: -ais/-aise, -ois/-oise, -ol/-ole, -ain/-aine, -ien/-ienne, -and/-ande. Give me a country and ask for both forms, and correct the doubled n in indienne, italienne, canadienne. ③ The preposition after aller: à + city, en + feminine country, au + masculine country, aux + plural country, à + tiny country like Monaco. Then reverse it with venir de: de France, du Japon, des États-Unis, d'Inde. Also check I know that only the person takes a capital letter (une Française) while the adjective and the language don't. Ask me about trips I've taken and want to take. Correct every attempt and finish with what to review.

title: Lire l'heure — reading the clock
goal: Ask the time, say any clock face out loud, and follow the 24-hour time France actually prints on tickets and appointment cards.

figures.alt: A clock face split in two. The right half, from twelve down to six, counts forward with « et » — et quart at fifteen minutes, et demie at thirty. The left half, from six back up to twelve, counts backwards from the next hour with « moins » — moins le quart at forty-five, moins dix at fifty. Beside the clock, the five positions written out, and a reminder that the twenty-four-hour clock never uses et quart, et demie or moins.
figures.caption: One clock, two directions. Past the half hour French stops counting up and starts counting down from the next hour — which is exactly what English does with « to ».

vocab.en: What time is it? (what you'll actually hear)
It's two o'clock — hear the z

vocab.fr: du matin / de l'après-midi / du soir
vocab.phonetic: dew ma-TAN / duh la-preh-mee-DEE / dew SWAHR
vocab.en: a.m. / in the afternoon / in the evening
a quarter of an hour — 15 minutes

grammar.point: « Il est » + the hour — then either « et » or « moins »

table.title: the clock has a forward half and a backward half

cells: Il est trois heures et quart
Il est trois heures et demie
Il est quatre heures moins le quart
Il est quatre heures moins dix

highlight: Il est quatre heures moins le quart
Il est quatre heures moins dix
table.note: Read down and watch the hour change at 3:45. Once you're past the half hour French abandons the hour you're in and counts backwards from the next one — « quatre heures moins le quart » is 3:45, not 4:45. English does the same thing with « to »; the only new habit is remembering to move the number up.

table2.title: the spoken clock and the printed one are different clocks

cells: deux heures et demie de l'après-midi
sept heures moins le quart du soir

table2.note: The 24-hour clock is what your train ticket, your cinema listing and your rendez-vous card will say — and it takes plain minutes only. No et quart, no et demie, no moins. Say « quinze heures quarante-cinq », never « quinze heures moins le quart ».

grammar.explain: The frame never changes: « il est » + the number + heure(s). One o'clock is « il est une heure » — heure is feminine, so it's une, not un — and from two o'clock on it takes an s you don't pronounce: deux heures, trois heures. What follows depends on which half of the clock you're in. ① Up to :30, add the minutes straight on: trois heures dix, trois heures et quart, trois heures et demie. ② After :30, jump to the next hour and subtract: quatre heures moins vingt, quatre heures moins le quart. Note the little asymmetry — you say « et quart » and « et demie » with et, but « moins le quart » with le. Midday and midnight get their own words, midi and minuit, and neither takes heures: « il est midi et demi ». To pin an event to a time you swap il est for à: « Le train part à huit heures. » And keep positions apart from lengths: « à huit heures et quart » is when something starts, « un quart d'heure » is how long it lasts.

notes.title: « et demie » drops its -e after midi and minuit
notes.body: Demie is an adjective agreeing with heure, which is feminine: « trois heures et demie ». But midi and minuit are masculine, so the -e goes: « midi et demi », « minuit et demi ». Written in front of a noun and hyphenated it never agrees at all — une demi-heure, une demi-journée, trois demi-litres.

notes.title: The liaison into « heures » is not optional
notes.body: Heure begins with a silent h, so the number before it links straight in: deux‿heures sounds « duh-ZUR », trois‿heures « trwah-ZUR », six‿heures « see-ZUR », dix‿heures « dee-ZUR », neuf heures « nuh-VUR » — the f turns into a v, one of only two words that does that to neuf (the other is neuf ans). Say « duh UR » and you sound like you're reading, not speaking.

notes.title: A position, or a length?
notes.body: « et quart » sits on the clock; « un quart d'heure » is a quantity of time. « Le film commence à huit heures et quart, il dure une heure et demie, et je suis arrivé un quart d'heure en retard. » Same three words, three different jobs — and only the middle one, une heure et demie, takes both.

notes.title: Nobody asks « quelle heure est-il ? » in a café
notes.body: It's correct, and it's what exams want. In the street you'll hear « Il est quelle heure ? » or « Vous avez l'heure ? » — literally, do you have the time. Both are polite; the second is the one to use on a stranger.

notes.title: Pile, environ, and the quarter-hour habit
notes.body: « Il est huit heures pile » is eight o'clock sharp. « Vers huit heures » or « huit heures environ » is around eight. And French really does think in quarter-hours — arrangements land on et quart, et demie and moins le quart far more often than on :10 or :20.

examples: — Quelle heure est-il ? — Il est trois heures et quart. (kel ur eh-TEEL ? eel eh trwah zur ay KAR)
Il est huit heures moins le quart, je suis en retard ! (eel eh weet ur mwan luh KAR)
Le train part à dix-huit heures quarante-cinq. (luh tran par ah dee-zweet ur ka-rahnt-SANK)
On déjeune à midi et demi ? (ohn day-ZHUN ah mee-dee ay duh-MEE)
J'ai rendez-vous chez le médecin à quatorze heures trente. (zhay rahn-day-VOO shay luh mayd-SAN ah ka-torz ur TRAHNT)
Le cours dure une heure et demie. (luh koor dewr ewn ur ay duh-MEE)
Je serai là dans un quart d'heure. (zhuh suh-ray lah dahn zuhn kar DUR)
practice: Careful with the hour: what is 7:45 in French? (not sept heures…)
Say the same three times twice — once spoken, once official: 14:15 · 19:30 · 21:45.
Fill in: « Il est midi ___ » and « Il est une heure ___ » (half past, both).
Position or length? Translate: « The class starts at half past nine and lasts an hour and a half. »
Answer out loud: « Tu te lèves à quelle heure ? » — then « Tu déjeunes à quelle heure ? »
tutorPrompt: Be my A1 French tutor for telling the time. Give me clock times one at a time — mix them, including plenty past the half hour — and have me say them in French. Correct three things hard: that after :30 I move to the next hour with « moins » (3:45 = quatre heures moins le quart), that « et demie » loses its -e after midi and minuit, and that I make the liaison in deux‿heures, trois‿heures, six‿heures, dix‿heures. Then switch to the 24-hour clock and check I stop using et quart / moins. Finish by asking me at what time I do four everyday things, and list the times I still got wrong.

title: Days, the week & making plans
goal: Name the days, split the day into its parts, and arrange to meet someone — the diary half of talking about time.

grammar.point: « lundi » or « le lundi » — one word, two different diaries

table.title: the article changes the appointment

rows.label: lundi
cells: this coming Monday — one specific day

rows.label: lundi prochain
cells: next Monday, said to remove all doubt

rows.label: tous les lundis
cells: every Monday — the emphatic version of « le lundi »

table.note: French needs no « on »: « je travaille lundi », not « je travaille sur lundi ». And days are never capitalised — lundi, janvier, français all stay lowercase, which will look wrong for months.

grammar.explain: Two habits. ① The bare day is a date, the day with « le » is a habit: « on se voit lundi » is an appointment, « le lundi, je travaille à la maison » is my week. ② Parts of the day attach straight onto the day with nothing in between: lundi matin, samedi soir, dimanche après-midi. Then, to fix a time, you need « à » and the clock — « on se voit jeudi à dix-neuf heures » — which the clock lesson before this one covers in full. Note also the pairs jour / journée, matin / matinée, soir / soirée and an / année: the short one is the point on the calendar, the long one is the stretch of time you lived through it. « Bonne journée » wishes someone a good day ahead; « bonjour » just says hello.

notes.title: The days are named after planets
notes.body: Five of them wear it openly: lundi is la Lune, mardi is Mars, mercredi is Mercure, jeudi is Jupiter, vendredi is Vénus, samedi is Saturne. Only dimanche broke the pattern — it was the sun's day, then Latin renamed it dies Dominicus, the Lord's day. Spot the -di and you can rebuild the whole week.

notes.title: « lundi » vs « le lundi »
notes.body: Without the article it means this coming Monday: « on se voit lundi ». With it, it means every Monday: « le lundi, je travaille à la maison ». One small word, completely different plan.

notes.title: jour or journée? an or année?
notes.body: The -ée forms measure the thing from the inside: « toute la journée » is all day long, « j'ai passé une bonne soirée » is I had a good evening. The short forms count: « trois jours », « deux ans », « ce soir ». So « bonne journée » as someone leaves, but « à demain, bonne soirée » if it's evening — and « j'ai vingt-cinq ans », never « années », when you give your age.

notes.title: Fixing the time itself
notes.body: Arranging to meet needs a clock as well as a day, and French speakers will give it to you on the 24-hour clock as often as not: « jeudi à dix-neuf heures trente ». That whole half — et quart, et demie, moins le quart, and the official times on your ticket — has its own lesson just before this one.

examples: — Tu es libre jeudi soir ? — Oui, ça me va. (tew eh LEE-bruh zhuh-dee SWAHR)
On se voit demain à midi ? — D'accord, à demain ! (ohn suh vwah duh-MAN ah mee-DEE)
Le lundi, je ne travaille pas. (luh luhn-DEE, zhuh nuh tra-VYE pa)
Samedi matin, je vais au marché. (sam-dee ma-TAN, zhuh veh oh mar-SHAY)
Mercredi est le jour de Mercure. (mer-kruh-DEE ay luh zhoor duh mer-KEWR)
Bonne journée ! — Merci, à vous aussi. (bon zhoor-NAY)
practice: Say the seven days in order, out loud, without looking.
Say what day it is today, what day it was yesterday, and what day it is tomorrow.
Which one means every week: « je joue au tennis mardi » or « le mardi » ?
Invite someone out for Saturday evening and propose a time.
Jour or journée? — « J'ai travaillé toute la ___ » · « Il reste trois ___ ».
Say three things you do « le week-end ».
tutorPrompt: Be my A1 French tutor for the days and making plans. Drill the seven days until they're automatic, then test the difference that costs people marks: « lundi » (this Monday) versus « le lundi » (every Monday). Check I never put a preposition in front of the day and never capitalise it. Then role-play arranging to meet: propose days and times, ask if I'm free, and make me counter-propose and confirm — « tu es libre jeudi ? », « ça te va ? », « on se dit à jeudi ». Slip in jour/journée and an/année at least once. Finish with what I should review.

title: Se repérer dans le temps — hier, maintenant, demain
goal: Place what you say in the past, the present or the future with the words French actually uses — and stop saying « actuellement » when you mean « actually ».

figures.alt: A timeline in three zones: passé on the left with il y a dix ans, le mois dernier, la semaine dernière, avant-hier and hier; présent in the middle with maintenant, aujourd'hui, en ce moment and actuellement; futur on the right with demain, après-demain, bientôt, la semaine prochaine and dans cinq ans. Below, an arrow shows « il y a » pointing back and « dans » pointing forward from the same present moment.
figures.caption: Three zones and one present moment. The middle column is where English speakers slip: actuellement means currently, and « actually » is en fait.

grammar.point: « Il y a » looks back, « dans » looks forward

table.title: every distance has a mirror image
table.note: Read across each row and only the last word moves: dernière → prochaine, il y a → dans. The middle of the timeline needs no mirror — maintenant, aujourd'hui, en ce moment and actuellement all sit on the present moment itself.

table2.title: the two little words that set the direction
table2.note: Both go in front of the amount of time, where English puts « ago » behind it: « il y a trois jours », never « trois jours il y a ». And « il y a » does two jobs — followed by a length of time it means ago, followed by a thing it means there is / there are.

grammar.explain: These words do the work a tense can't: they say when. French sorts them into three zones. ① Le passé: hier, avant-hier, la semaine dernière, le mois dernier, and « il y a + a length of time » for anything further back. ② Le présent: maintenant, aujourd'hui, en ce moment, actuellement — the last two both mean « right now, these days », and they're what you use for the situation you're living in. ③ Le futur: demain, après-demain, bientôt, la semaine prochaine, and « dans + a length of time » for anything further ahead. Two habits to build. Dernier and prochain come after the noun — « la semaine prochaine », not « la prochaine semaine ». And il y a / dans both come before the number, unlike English « ago ». Drop any of these at the front of a sentence, add a comma, and the rest of the sentence stays exactly as it was: « Demain, je travaille. »

notes.title: « Actuellement » does not mean « actually »
notes.body: It means currently. « Actuellement, j'habite à Paris » = right now, these days, I live in Paris. English « actually » is « en fait » or « en réalité »: « En fait, je ne suis pas d'accord. » The whole family behaves this way — actuel means current, and l'actualité is the news. One more from the same trap: éventuellement means possibly, not eventually (that's finalement).

notes.title: dernier and prochain sit after the noun
notes.body: La semaine dernière, le mois prochain, l'année dernière, le week-end prochain — French puts them where English can't. Put them in front and the meaning shifts: « la dernière semaine de janvier » is the final week of January, not last week.

notes.title: French builds two days out with one word
notes.body: avant + hier = avant-hier, après + demain = après-demain. Both keep the hyphen, and the -s of après stays silent. English needs five words for each, which is why they feel so satisfying to say.

notes.title: You'll need these before you need the past tense
notes.body: The past tense itself is A2 — passé composé, two lessons away. But the markers come first, because they're what makes a past sentence legible: hear « il y a huit mois » or « la semaine dernière » and you already know where in time the story sits, whatever the verb is doing.

examples: Actuellement, j'habite à Paris. (ak-tew-el-MAHN, zha-BEET ah pa-REE)
En ce moment, je cherche un appartement. (ahn suh mo-MAHN, zhuh SHEHRSH uhn na-par-tuh-MAHN)
Nous sommes arrivés il y a huit mois. (noo som za-ree-VAY eel ee ah wee MWAH)
Après-demain, je vais voir un ami. (ah-preh-duh-MAN, zhuh veh vwahr uhn na-MEE)
La semaine prochaine, on va déménager. (lah suh-men pro-SHEN, ohn va day-may-na-ZHAY)
— Tu pars quand ? — Bientôt, dans deux jours. (byan-TOH, dahn duh ZHOOR)
practice: Sort these into passé / présent / futur: bientôt · avant-hier · en ce moment · le mois dernier · dans deux jours.
Say three true sentences about yourself: one with hier, one with maintenant, one with demain.
Fill both gaps: « ___ trois ans » (three years ago) · « ___ trois ans » (in three years).
Translate carefully: « Actually, I'm not French. » — and not with actuellement.
Flip them forward: la semaine dernière → ___ , le mois dernier → ___ , avant-hier → ___ .
Answer out loud: « Tu es arrivé en France quand ? »
tutorPrompt: Be my A1 French tutor for placing things in time. Drill the three zones: passé (hier, avant-hier, la semaine dernière, le mois dernier, il y a + durée), présent (maintenant, aujourd'hui, en ce moment, actuellement) and futur (demain, après-demain, bientôt, la semaine prochaine, dans + durée). Test two traps hard: « il y a » versus « dans » for the same distance in opposite directions, and « actuellement » = currently, never « actually » (which is en fait / en réalité). Also check that I put dernier and prochain after the noun. Ask me simple questions about when I do things, one at a time, and correct every answer. Finish with the markers I still get wrong.

title: Depuis, pendant, il y a, dans — how long, and when
goal: Say how long something has been going on, how long it lasted, and when it happened — with the four little words French sorts this with, and the tense each one demands.

figures.alt: A timeline with « maintenant » marked in the middle. « Il y a » points back to a single dot in the past. « Depuis » is a solid bar running from a dot in the past right up to now and continuing past it. « Pendant » is a closed block sitting entirely inside the past, with a start and an end. « Dans » points forward to a single dot in the future. Below, the tense rule: depuis takes the present, pendant takes the passé composé.
figures.caption: Two of them mark a point — il y a behind you, dans ahead of you. Two of them measure a stretch — depuis is still running, pendant is finished.

vocab.en: It's been two years that… (spoken « depuis »)

grammar.point: Four words, four shapes on the timeline

table.title: what each one actually marks

rows.label: il y a
cells: J'ai rencontré Pierre il y a dix ans.

rows.label: depuis
cells: J'habite à Paris depuis dix ans.

rows.label: pendant
cells: Hier, il a plu pendant cinq heures.

rows.label: dans
cells: Je pars en vacances dans une semaine.

highlight: J'habite à Paris depuis dix ans.
Hier, il a plu pendant cinq heures.
table.note: Depuis and pendant both translate as English « for », which is why they get mixed up. The test is whether it's over. Still true now → depuis. Finished → pendant.

table2.title: each word drags a tense along with it

rows.label: depuis
cells: Je travaille ici depuis trois ans.

rows.label: pendant
cells: J'ai travaillé ici pendant trois ans.

rows.label: il y a
cells: J'ai commencé il y a trois ans.

highlight: Je travaille ici depuis trois ans.
table2.note: The first row is the one to burn in. English says « I have been working here for three years » with a past-shaped verb; French says « je travaille » in the plain present, because you're still working there. Swap to the past and you've quit.

grammar.explain: All four answer a « when » or a « how long », and French keeps their jobs strictly apart. ① Il y a + a length of time = ago. It goes in front of the amount, where English puts « ago » behind it: « il y a dix ans », never « dix ans il y a ». ② Dans + a length of time = in, counting forward from now: « dans une semaine ». ③ Depuis = the action started back then and hasn't stopped, so the verb stays in the present: « j'habite à Paris depuis dix ans » — I have been living in Paris for ten years, and I still do. Depuis also takes a starting point rather than a length: depuis 2025, depuis lundi, depuis mon arrivée. ④ Pendant = a measured stretch, opened and closed, so the verb goes into the past: « j'ai habité à Paris pendant dix ans » — and I don't any more. Two things worth knowing beyond the four. Pendant is often simply dropped when the duration follows the verb — « j'ai attendu deux heures » is perfectly normal French. And « pour » looks like pendant but points forward at a plan: « je pars à Nice pour une semaine » is how long I intend to stay, not how long I stayed.

notes.title: « Ça fait… que » is what people actually say
notes.body: « Ça fait dix ans que j'habite à Paris » means exactly « j'habite à Paris depuis dix ans » — it just moves the duration to the front of the sentence, which is where the emphasis wants to be. The verb still stays in the present. There's a formal cousin too, « Il y a dix ans que j'habite à Paris », where il y a for once does not mean ago.

notes.title: Two questions that look identical in English
notes.body: « Depuis combien de temps tu apprends le français ? » asks how long you've been at it and still are — answer with the present: « depuis huit mois ». « Pendant combien de temps as-tu appris le français ? » asks about a finished period — answer in the past: « pendant deux ans ». The English is « how long » both times. The French chooses for you, and the tense you answer in has to match.

notes.title: Depuis with a negative flips into « not since »
notes.body: « Je n'ai pas vu Marie depuis trois mois » — I haven't seen Marie for three months. This is the one place depuis takes the passé composé rather than the present, because the verb is negative: nothing has been happening. « Je ne fume plus depuis 2020. »

notes.title: Il y a does two completely different jobs
notes.body: Followed by a length of time it means ago: « il y a trois jours ». Followed by a thing it means there is / there are: « il y a du pain sur la table ». Same three words. Only what comes next tells you which one you're hearing — and it's almost never ambiguous in practice.

notes.title: Where you'll need this first
notes.body: The very first questions anyone asks a newcomer: « Vous êtes en France depuis combien de temps ? » and « Vous êtes arrivés quand ? ». One wants depuis and the present, the other wants il y a and the passé composé. Have both answers ready and the conversation moves on to something more interesting.

examples: J'habite à Paris depuis huit mois. (zha-BEET ah pa-REE duh-pwee wee MWAH)
Nous sommes arrivés il y a huit mois. (noo som za-ree-VAY eel ee ah wee MWAH)
J'ai étudié le français pendant deux ans à Delhi. (zhay ay-tew-dee-AY luh frahn-SEH pahn-dahn duh ZAHN)
Ça fait deux heures que je t'attends ! (sa feh duh zur kuh zhuh ta-TAHN)
— Depuis combien de temps tu apprends le français ? — Depuis un an. (duh-pwee kohn-byan duh TAHN)
Je pars en Inde dans trois semaines, pour un mois. (zhuh par ahn AND dahn trwah suh-MEN, poor uhn MWAH)
Je n'ai pas vu mes parents depuis Noël. (zhuh nay pa vew may pa-RAHN duh-pwee no-EL)
practice: Choose: « J'apprends le français ___ six mois » — depuis or pendant?
Now change one word so it means you've stopped. What else has to change?
Fill both: « Je suis arrivé ___ un an » (a year ago) · « Je repars ___ un an » (in a year).
Answer for real, out loud: « Vous êtes en France depuis combien de temps ? »
Rewrite with « ça fait… que »: « Je travaille ici depuis trois ans. »
Translate carefully: « I haven't spoken French since Monday. » (mind the tense)
Say one true sentence with each of the four: il y a, depuis, pendant, dans.
tutorPrompt: Be my A1 French tutor for depuis, pendant, il y a and dans. Drill the split that English hides: depuis = still going, so the verb stays in the PRESENT; pendant = finished, so the verb goes into the passé composé. Ask me « depuis combien de temps… ? » and « pendant combien de temps… ? » questions alternately and correct my tense every single time, not just my word choice. Also check I put il y a and dans before the amount of time, and test « ça fait… que » as a rewrite. Ask about my life in France, my French learning, and my last holiday. Finish by listing which of the four I still misuse.

title: Les mois & la date — quelle est la date d'aujourd'hui ?
goal: Name the twelve months, say today's date the way people really say it, and read the dd/mm dates on every French form and ticket.

vocab.en: It's the sixth of August. (the everyday answer)

vocab.fr: C'est le six août deux mille vingt-six.
vocab.phonetic: seh luh see-zoot duh meel vant-SEESS

vocab.en: the first of May (the only ordinal)

vocab.fr: en mai / au mois de mai
vocab.phonetic: ahn MEH / oh mwah duh MEH

vocab.fr: Mon anniversaire, c'est le douze mars.
vocab.phonetic: mo na-nee-vehr-SEHR, seh luh dooz MARSS
vocab.en: My birthday is the twelfth of March.

grammar.point: The date is one formula: le + a plain number + the month

table.title: everything you need for a date
table.note: English says « the sixth of August ». French throws away both the ordinal and the « of »: « le six août ». Only the 1st resists — le premier, written 1er. The longer question « Quelle est la date d'aujourd'hui ? » works too, and « au mois de mai » is a longer way of saying « en mai ».

table2.title: saying the year out loud
table2.note: French counts the year as one whole number — never « vingt vingt-six » the way English says twenty twenty-six. And mille stays bare: deux mille, never « deux milles ». Years before 2000 keep the same logic, they're just longer: 1990 is « mille neuf cent quatre-vingt-dix ».

grammar.explain: Three things and the date is yours. ① The months are never capitalised: janvier, février, mars… Writing « Janvier » is one of the most visible English habits in a French text. ② The formula is le + number + month, with no ordinal and no de: « le six août », « le vingt-cinq décembre ». The single exception is the 1st, which takes premier — « le premier mai », written « le 1er mai ». ③ For « in » a month, use en or au mois de: « en août », « au mois d'août » — never dans, which is for the future (« dans deux mois » = in two months' time). Add the year on the end as one long number and you have the full date: « le premier mai deux mille vingt-six ». To ask, « Quelle est la date d'aujourd'hui ? » and to answer, either « On est le… » or « C'est le… » — both are everywhere.

notes.title: 06/08/2026 is the sixth of August
notes.body: France writes dates day/month/year, on every form, ticket, prescription and appointment card. Read 06/08 the American way and you'll turn up two months early — or miss a flight. When it matters, write the month in letters: 6 août 2026.

notes.title: The three months that trip everyone up
notes.body: août looks like three vowels and comes out as « oot » — often just « oo ». juin is one syllable, « zhwan », and juillet is two, « zhwee-yeh »; mixing them up moves your appointment by a month. And the -s of mars is pronounced, unlike most final consonants: « marss ».

notes.title: En août, la France ferme
notes.body: August is when the country goes on holiday — bakeries, doctors, your local boulangerie all put a note on the door: « Fermeture annuelle du 1er au 31 août ». Worth being able to read that sentence before you need it. Note the liaison too: « en août » runs together as « ah-NOOT ».

examples: — Quelle est la date d'aujourd'hui ? — On est le six août. (ohn eh luh see-ZOOT)
Mon anniversaire, c'est le premier mai. (mo na-nee-vehr-SEHR, seh luh pruh-mee-AY MEH)
Je suis arrivée en France en décembre. (zhuh swee za-ree-VAY ahn frahnss ahn day-SAHM-bruh)
Le rendez-vous est le douze mars à quatorze heures. (luh dooz marss ah ka-torz UR)
En août, beaucoup de magasins sont fermés. (ah-NOOT, boh-koo duh ma-ga-ZAN sohn fehr-MAY)
Nous sommes en deux mille vingt-six. (noo som ahn duh meel vant-SEESS)
practice: Say today's date out loud, both ways: « On est le… » and « C'est le… ».
Say your birthday, then the birthdays of two people you know.
Read these aloud in full: 01/01 · 14/07 · 25/12.
Name the month before février and the month after septembre.
Say the month and the year you arrived in France.
Careful with the 1st: « le ___ janvier », and with « in »: « ___ janvier ».
tutorPrompt: Be my A1 French tutor for months and dates. Drill the twelve months, especially the pronunciation of août, juin, juillet and mars. Ask me « Quelle est la date d'aujourd'hui ? » and make me answer with both « On est le… » and « C'est le… ». Test that I use premier for the 1st and plain numbers for every other day, that I don't capitalise months, that I say « en août » and not « dans août », and that I read years as one number (deux mille vingt-six). Give me dd/mm dates like 06/08 and 14/07 to read out in full, and ask me for birthdays and appointment dates. Correct each attempt and end with what to review.

title: Family & your daily routine
goal: Describe your family and talk about your everyday routine in the present tense.

grammar.point: mon, ma, mes — possessives agree with the thing owned, not the owner

table.title: picking between mon, ma and mes
table.note: The last row is the surprise: amie is feminine, but « ma amie » is unsayable, so French switches to mon for the liaison. Same for mon école, mon adresse.

table2.title: the whole set
table2.note: notre, votre and leur don't bother with gender — one form for masculine and feminine, and only the plural changes.

grammar.explain: The rule that catches every English speaker: a French possessive agrees with the thing being owned, not with the person who owns it. « mon frère » and « ma sœur » both mean my — the word changed because frère is masculine and sœur is feminine, not because of anything about me. Plural is mes for both genders. One extra wrinkle: a feminine word starting with a vowel takes mon rather than ma, purely so the two words can run together — mon amie, mon école. For the verbs in this lesson (habiter, travailler, parler), the -er endings are laid out in « The two patterns you can predict ».

notes.title: « sa femme » doesn't tell you whose
notes.body: Because the possessive agrees with the thing owned, son and sa carry no information about the owner. « sa femme » is his wife or her wife; « son mari » is her husband or his husband. If it genuinely matters, French adds « à lui » or « à elle » — but usually the context has already settled it.

notes.title: mon / ton / son before a vowel
notes.body: It's not just mon. Any feminine word starting with a vowel takes the masculine-looking form: mon amie, ton école, son adresse. The word is still feminine — « mon amie est gentille », with the feminine adjective — only the possessive changed shape.

notes.title: Where the verb endings live
notes.body: This lesson uses habiter, travailler and parler, all 1st group. If the endings aren't automatic yet, the full pattern for both regular groups is in « The two patterns you can predict — conjugating -er and -ir verbs », two lessons further on.

examples: J'habite à Paris avec mon mari. Je parle anglais et un peu français.
Le matin, je me lève à sept heures et je travaille à la maison.
Ma sœur habite à Londres avec ses deux enfants. (say duh zahn-FAHN)
Mon amie Claire travaille à la mairie. (mohn na-MEE)
Nos parents viennent nous voir en août. (noh pa-RAHN)
practice: Introduce two members of your family, with the right possessive each time.
mon, ma or mes? « ___ père » · « ___ mère » · « ___ enfants » · « ___ amie » · « ___ famille ».
Say it in French: his sister, her sister. What do you notice?
Swap to « your (tu) »: mon frère → ___ , ma sœur → ___ , mes parents → ___ .
Describe your morning in three sentences, then say who else is in the house.
tutorPrompt: A1 French conversation about family and daily routine. Ask me about my family and my day, one simple question at a time (where I live, who I live with, what I do in a day). Drill the possessives hard while we talk: mon/ma/mes, ton/ta/tes, son/sa/ses, notre/nos, votre/vos, leur/leurs. Check I understand that the possessive agrees with the thing owned and not the owner — so « sa femme » can be his wife or her wife — and that feminine words starting with a vowel take mon/ton/son (mon amie, son école). Correct me every time I pick the wrong one. After about eight questions, give me feedback and five words to remember.

title: Les adverbes de fréquence — toujours, souvent, jamais
goal: Say how often you do something, from every single time down to never — and put the word in the place French wants it, which is not where English puts it.

figures.alt: A scale from 100 percent down to 0 percent with five French adverbs beside it: toujours at 100 percent, souvent at 75, parfois at 50, rarement at 25 and ne… jamais at 0. Below, the placement rule: the adverb goes after the conjugated verb, as in je vais souvent au cinéma.
figures.caption: Five words cover the whole scale. Only the bottom one needs help: jamais brings « ne » with it, because zero is a negative.

vocab.en: I often go to the cinema.

vocab.fr: Je ne bois jamais de café.
vocab.phonetic: zhuh nuh bwah zha-meh duh ka-FAY

grammar.point: The adverb goes after the verb, not in front of it

table.title: the scale, top to bottom

cells: je mange rarement de la viande
je ne mange jamais de viande

table.note: Notice where the word sits in every single example: straight after the conjugated verb. English says « I often go », French says « je vais souvent ». Putting it between the subject and the verb — « je souvent vais » — is the one placement that's simply wrong.

table2.title: how the negative one behaves

rows.label: not
cells: je ne bois pas de café

rows.label: never
cells: je ne bois jamais de café

highlight: je ne bois jamais de café
table2.note: jamais simply takes the place of pas in the frame you already know: ne … pas becomes ne … jamais. And the du/de la/des → de rule still applies, because it's still a negative: « du café » becomes « de café ».

grammar.explain: Five words carry the whole scale from every time to no times: toujours, souvent, parfois, rarement, jamais. Two things to get right. ① Placement. In a simple sentence the adverb comes immediately after the conjugated verb — « je vais souvent au cinéma », « il est toujours en retard », « nous prenons rarement le train ». Longer expressions of frequency behave differently: tous les jours, une fois par semaine and de temps en temps prefer the beginning or the end of the sentence — « tous les jours, je me lève à sept heures ». ② Jamais is a negative, so it needs ne in front of the verb, exactly like pas: « je ne fais jamais la cuisine ». Answering a question with a bare « Jamais ! » is fine, because there's no verb left to negate.

notes.title: Not where English puts it
notes.body: English slips the adverb in before the verb — I always eat, I often go. French puts it after: « je mange toujours », « je vais souvent ». Say a few out loud in the French order until it stops sounding wrong, because word order is the part that gives you away long after the vocabulary is solid.

notes.title: « toujours » has a second meaning
notes.body: Most of the time it means always. But with a present tense and the right context it means still: « tu es toujours là ? » is are you still there?, not are you always there. Context settles it, and « encore » is the word to use when you really need to say still: « tu es encore là ? »

notes.title: jamais keeps the whole negative frame
notes.body: The ne is compulsory in writing, and it drops out in speech just like it does with pas: « je vais jamais au gym ». The article rule survives too — « je ne bois jamais de vin », never « du vin ». Everything you learned in « Saying no » applies unchanged; only the second word swaps.

notes.title: Counting is a different shape
notes.body: For an exact count, French uses fois: une fois par jour, deux fois par semaine, trois fois par mois, plusieurs fois par an. These aren't adverbs, so they don't sit after the verb — they go at the start or the end: « je fais du sport deux fois par semaine ».

examples: Je vais souvent au marché le samedi. (zhuh veh soo-vahn oh mar-SHAY luh sam-DEE)
Il est toujours en retard. (ee leh too-zhoor ahn ruh-TAR)
Je ne bois jamais de café après midi. (zhuh nuh bwah zha-meh duh ka-FAY)
Nous allons rarement au restaurant. (noo za-lohn rar-mahn oh res-toh-RAHN)
De temps en temps, on prend le train pour Lyon. (duh tahn zahn TAHN)
Je fais du sport deux fois par semaine. (duh fwah par suh-MEN)
practice: Put them in order, 100% to 0%: rarement · toujours · jamais · souvent · parfois.
Fix the word order: « je souvent vais au cinéma » → ___ .
Say three true sentences about yourself with souvent, rarement and jamais.
Make it never: « je bois du vin » → ___ (careful with du).
Answer out loud: « Tu fais souvent la cuisine ? »
Say how often you do two things, using « fois par semaine ».
tutorPrompt: Be my A1 French tutor for adverbs of frequency. Drill the scale — toujours (100%), souvent (75%), parfois / quelquefois (50%), rarement (25%), ne… jamais (0%) — plus de temps en temps and the fois expressions (une fois par semaine, deux fois par mois). Test placement hard: in French the adverb goes immediately after the conjugated verb (« je vais souvent au cinéma »), never between subject and verb, while the longer expressions go at the start or the end of the sentence. Check that I use ne with jamais and that I turn du/de la/des into de after it (« je ne bois jamais de café »). Ask me how often I do everyday things — sport, cooking, the cinema, speaking French — one question at a time, and make me answer with a different adverb each time. Correct every answer and finish with the ones I placed wrongly.

title: Le visage — the face & the verbs of the senses
goal: Name every part of a face, describe someone so they'd be recognised, and use the five verbs of perception — including the pairs French keeps apart that English doesn't.

figures.alt: A labelled face showing les cheveux, le crâne, le front, le sourcil, l'œil, le nez, l'oreille, la narine, la joue, les lèvres, la bouche, le menton and le cou
figures.caption: Thirteen labels, and one completely irregular plural: un œil becomes des yeux — no other word in the lesson changes shape like that.

vocab.en: I hear / I smell / I see — they just happen
I listen / I watch — on purpose

grammar.point: Five senses, five body parts, five verbs

table.title: the sense, the part, the verb
table.note: The three highlighted verbs are 3rd group and irregular — they get their own table below. goûter and toucher are ordinary 1st group, so they already follow a pattern you know.

table2.title: the three irregular ones
table2.note: entendre and sentir keep one stem throughout. voir switches to voy- at nous and vous, then to voi- again at ils. All three sound identical across je, tu and il.

grammar.explain: A face is mostly vocabulary, but three things are worth real attention. ① un œil → des yeux is the most irregular plural in everyday French; nothing about the singular predicts the plural, so learn them as two separate words. ② The senses each pair a body part with a verb, and two of those verbs come in pairs English merges: entendre is to hear (it reaches your ears) while écouter is to listen (you chose to); voir is to see while regarder is to watch. Mixing them up is one of the clearest markers of a beginner. ③ French describes bodies with le, la, les — not with mon, ma, mes. « J'ai mal à la tête », not « à ma tête ».

notes.title: Body parts take le, not mon
notes.body: This is the flip side of the possessives you just learned. French says « j'ai mal à la tête », « elle a les yeux bleus », « il se lave les mains » — the definite article, where English insists on my, her, his. Using the possessive isn't wrong so much as odd, and it marks you out immediately.

notes.title: entendre vs écouter, voir vs regarder
notes.body: The first of each pair just happens to you; the second is something you do on purpose. « J'entends la musique » — I can hear it, whether I like it or not. « J'écoute la musique » — I'm listening. Same with « je vois la mer » (it's in front of me) and « je regarde la mer » (I'm watching it).

notes.title: sentir does three jobs
notes.body: « Je sens une odeur » — I smell something. « Ça sent bon » — it smells good. And with a reflexive, « je me sens bien » — I feel well. One verb, three uses, and context tells them apart.

notes.title: les cheveux is always plural
notes.body: Hair on your head is les cheveux — « elle a les cheveux courts ». Un cheveu is one single strand, the kind you find in your soup. Same shape as un œil / des yeux: the singular exists but almost never comes up.

examples: Elle a les yeux bleus et les cheveux courts. (lay ZYUH BLUH)
J'entends la musique mais je n'écoute pas. (zhahn-TAHN lah mew-ZEEK)
Ça sent bon dans la cuisine ! (sah sahn BOHN)
Il a mal à la tête depuis ce matin. (eel ah mal ah lah TET)
Nous voyons la mer depuis la fenêtre. (noo vwah-YOHN lah MEHR)
Tu veux goûter ce fromage ? (tew vuh goo-TAY)

entendre or écouter? « Je ___ la radio tous les matins » · « Tu ___ ce bruit ? »
voir or regarder? « Je ___ un film ce soir » · « D'ici on ___ la tour Eiffel ».
Fill in: nous ___ (voir) · ils ___ (entendre) · vous ___ (sentir).

Drill the vocabulary with articles: le visage, les cheveux, le crâne, le front, le sourcil, l'œil, l'oreille, le nez, la narine, la joue, la pommette, la bouche, les lèvres, le menton, le cou, la nuque, la barbe, la moustache. Also check I use the definite article for body parts — « j'ai mal à la tête », not « à ma tête ». Finish by having me describe a person's face, and correct my genders.

title: Le corps — from head to toe
goal: Name the body from head to foot, and say what hurts — the sentence you'll need before you need any other.

grammar.point: « avoir mal à » — and what à does to the article

table.title: à + the article, which is where this goes wrong
table.note: Only two of the five change shape: à + le becomes au, à + les becomes aux. À la and à l' stay exactly as they are. Get the gender of the body part right and the rest is automatic.

table2.title: French says « the », where English says « my »

rows.label: injury
cells: je me suis cassé le bras

highlight: je me suis cassé le bras
table2.note: With your own body French uses the plain article. It can afford to: « j'ai » or the reflexive « me » has already said whose body it is, so « mon » would be saying it twice. « Je me lave mes mains » is the giveaway of an English speaker.

grammar.explain: One frame does nearly all the work: avoir mal à + the body part. It is avoir, not être — « j'ai mal », never « je suis mal », which means something closer to I'm unwell in myself. Then à collides with the article: à + le = au (j'ai mal au dos, au ventre, au genou, au pied), à + la stays à la (à la tête, à la jambe, à la main, à la gorge), à + l' before a vowel (à l'épaule, à l'oreille), à + les = aux (aux jambes, aux dents, aux pieds). So the only thing you really have to memorise per word is its gender — the contraction follows on its own. Two ways to intensify it: « j'ai très mal » and « j'ai un peu mal ». And when the doctor asks, the question is « Où avez-vous mal ? » or « Qu'est-ce qui ne va pas ? » — answer with the same frame and you're understood.

notes.title: The silent endings are the whole difficulty
notes.body: le corps (« kor »), le bras (« brah »), le dos (« doh »), le pied (« pyay »), le doigt (« dwah »). Five common words, five endings you write and never say. The plural changes nothing you can hear either: le bras / les bras is the same sound twice, and only the article tells you how many.

notes.title: le genou → les genoux
notes.body: Genou is one of the seven -ou nouns that take -x instead of -s in the plural: bijou, caillou, chou, genou, hibou, joujou, pou — jewel, pebble, cabbage, knee, owl, toy, louse. French children learn them as a nonsense sentence and so can you; it's the whole list, there are no others.

notes.title: « avoir mal à » vs « faire mal »
notes.body: « J'ai mal au dos » — I have a sore back, said from the inside. « Mon dos me fait mal » — my back is hurting me, said about the back. And « se faire mal » is to hurt yourself: « je me suis fait mal au genou ». All three are common; the first is the one to reach for by default.

notes.title: l'épaule is feminine, le cœur isn't
notes.body: Hearing l' tells you nothing about gender, so these two are worth fixing early: une épaule, à l'épaule, mais aussi « j'ai mal aux épaules ». Le cœur is masculine — au cœur — and it turns up in more idioms than anatomy: avoir mal au cœur means to feel sick, not to have heart trouble. That one has caught out a lot of tourists.

notes.title: A hand's worth of extras
notes.body: Below the ones on the diagram: le poignet (wrist), le coude (elbow), la cheville (ankle), l'orteil (toe), la peau (skin), le sang (blood), l'os (bone — « oss » in the singular, but « oh » in the plural, les os). You won't need them today. You'll want them at the pharmacie.

— Où avez-vous mal ? — J'ai mal au dos, docteur. (oo a-vay voo MAL ? zhay mal oh DOH)
Il a mal aux jambes après le marathon. (eel ah mal oh ZHAHMB)
Je me suis fait mal au genou. (zhuh muh swee feh mal oh zhuh-NOO)
Elle s'est cassé le bras en tombant. (el seh ka-SAY luh BRAH ahn tohn-BAHN)
Lave-toi les mains avant de manger. (lav-twah lay MAN a-vahn duh mahn-ZHAY)
J'ai mal au cœur en voiture. (zhay mal oh KUR ahn vwah-TEWR)

tutorPrompt: Be my A1 French tutor for the body and « avoir mal à ». Name body parts and have me give them with the right article, then have me build « j'ai mal… » sentences. title: The map — every French tense on one line
goal: See the whole verb system at once, learn the three shortcuts that need no new conjugation at all, and find out how few tenses you actually need to hold a conversation.

figures.alt: The verb manger in ten tenses down a single rail, grouped into le passé, le présent and le futur, each with its French form, its English meaning, and a badge showing the level at which you meet it
figures.caption: Ten shapes of one verb, in time order. The filled badges are the ones you meet in A1 and A2 — four of the ten. Everything else can wait.

vocab.en: I eat / I'm eating — le présent

vocab.fr: je suis en train de manger
vocab.phonetic: zhuh swee zahn tran duh mahn-ZHAY

vocab.en: I've just eaten — le passé récent
I'm going to eat — le futur proche
I ate / I have eaten — le passé composé
I will eat — le futur simple

grammar.point: Three of them need no new conjugation — a verb you know, plus the infinitive

table.title: one small verb + manger, and you have three more tenses

rows.label: être en train de
cells: je suis en train de manger

table.note: Venir, être and aller are verbs you already know, and manger never changes — it stays in the infinitive. So these three cost you nothing new, and between them they cover the recent past, the live present and the near future. « Je viens d'arriver », « je vais partir », « je suis en train de travailler »: swap the infinitive and the pattern holds for every verb in French.

table2.title: the three that carry a conversation
table2.note: Everything else on the map is refinement. With these three, plus « je viens de » for something that just happened, you can already say what you did yesterday, what you're doing now and what you'll do tomorrow — which is most of what anyone says.

grammar.explain: French verbs look like a long list of tenses, and the list is what makes them feel heavy. The map turns the list back into what it really is: one verb, seen from different distances in time. Read it top to bottom and you're walking from the deep past to the far future. Three things are worth noticing. ① You need very few of them. Four of the ten are A1–A2, and three of those four do almost all the work. ② Three of them aren't really new tenses at all — venir de, être en train de and aller each take a verb you already have and bolt an infinitive on the end, so you can talk about just-now, right-now and soon before you've conjugated a single past or future. ③ The heavy-looking ones at the two ends — plus-que-parfait, futur antérieur — are for writing and for B2. Nobody is going to stop you in the street with « j'aurai mangé ».

notes.title: You can talk about the past before you learn a past tense
notes.body: « Je viens de » + infinitive means it happened a moment ago: « je viens de manger », « je viens d'arriver », « on vient de rentrer ». That's the whole rule. It only works for the very recent past — for yesterday you need the passé composé — but for the first months it fills the gap beautifully.

notes.title: French has one présent where English has two
notes.body: « Je mange » is both I eat and I am eating. There's no separate continuous tense, so don't go looking for one. If you really need to stress that it's happening this second — someone rings while you're at the table — say « je suis en train de manger ».

notes.title: Why the past has two entries
notes.body: English uses one past for both; French splits the job. Passé composé is for a finished event: « hier, j'ai mangé au restaurant ». Imparfait is for a background or a habit: « quand j'étais petite, je mangeais beaucoup de riz ». You don't have to choose between them yet — but knowing the split is coming makes it much less of a shock at B1.

notes.title: Where each one lives on this site
notes.body: Le présent is the next two lessons in this module. Le passé composé and le futur proche are in A2, Everyday life. L'imparfait, le futur simple and l'impératif are in B1, Finding your voice. Le plus-que-parfait waits until B2. Come back to this map whenever a new tense turns up and put it in its place.

examples: Je mange à midi tous les jours. (zhuh mahnzh ah mee-DEE too lay ZHOOR)
— Tu as faim ? — Non merci, je viens de manger. (zhuh vyan duh mahn-ZHAY)
Je suis en train de travailler, je te rappelle. (zhuh swee zahn tran duh tra-va-YAY)
Ce soir, je vais manger avec des amis. (suh SWAHR, zhuh veh mahn-ZHAY)
Hier, j'ai mangé au restaurant. (ee-YEHR, zhay mahn-ZHAY oh res-toh-RAHN)
Nous venons d'arriver en France. (noo vuh-nohn da-ree-VAY ahn FRAHNSS)

Without looking: which three tenses do you actually need this month?
tutorPrompt: Be my A1 French tutor for the shape of the French verb system. Don't drill conjugations — drill placement. Give me a French sentence and ask me where it sits in time (passé, présent, futur) and which form it uses: je mange, je viens de manger, je suis en train de manger, je vais manger, j'ai mangé, je mangeais, je mangerai. title: The three verb groups — how French verbs sort themselves
goal: Look at any infinitive and know which of the three groups it belongs to — so you know whether its endings are predictable or need learning by heart.

figures.alt: A decision tree in English: does the infinitive end in -er? If yes and it is not aller, first group. If not, does it end in -ir? If no, third group. If yes, does nous end in -issons? If yes, second group; if no, third group.
figures.caption: Three questions sort every French verb. Note that the 2nd group needs both answers — an -ir infinitive AND -issons at « nous ». Question ③ is where partir and courir fall out into the 3rd group.

grammar.point: Ask two questions and every verb lands in a group

table.title: the three groups
table.note: The 1st group is by far the biggest — about 90% of French verbs — and it's fully predictable. The 3rd group is small but contains the verbs you use every day.

table2.title: the -ir trap: -ir alone is not enough
table2.note: Every verb here ends in -ir, so the ending alone decides nothing. The 2nd group needs the -ir AND -issons at nous; miss the second condition and the verb is 3rd group.

grammar.explain: French sorts its verbs into three groups, and the group tells you whether the endings are predictable. ① 1st group: the infinitive ends in -er. Drop -er, add -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent. This is the huge, safe group — and aller is its single deserter. ② 2nd group: the infinitive ends in -ir and the nous form ends in -issons. finir → nous finissons, choisir → nous choisissons. ③ 3rd group: everything else — the remaining -ir verbs, all the -oir and -re verbs, and aller. These are irregular and learnt one at a time. The whole system turns on the nous form, which is why it's worth learning a new verb as a pair: the infinitive and its nous.

notes.title: Not every -ir verb is 2nd group
notes.body: This is the mistake the classification exists to catch. finir makes nous finissons, so it's 2nd group. But partir makes nous partons, courir makes nous courons, and venir makes nous venons — no -issons, so all three are 3rd group and irregular. The infinitive looks identical; only the nous form tells you.

notes.title: aller ends in -er and still isn't 1st group
notes.body: It's the one exception to the -er rule, and a big one: je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont. Nothing about that follows the parler pattern, which is why aller is filed with the irregulars.

notes.title: nous mangeons keeps its e
notes.body: A spelling detail inside the 1st group: verbs in -ger keep the e before -ons (nous mangeons, nous voyageons) and verbs in -cer take a cedilla (nous commençons). Without it, the g and c would harden and the word would sound wrong.

examples: Nous parlons français à la maison. (noo par-LOHN frahn-SEH)
Nous finissons le travail à six heures. (noo fee-nee-SOHN)
Nous partons demain matin. (noo par-TOHN duh-MAN)
Nous prenons le métro ensemble. (noo pruh-NOHN)
Nous allons au marché le samedi. (noo za-LOHN oh mar-SHAY)
Attention : tous les verbes en -ir ne sont pas du deuxième groupe. (dew duh-zee-EM GROOP)

tutorPrompt: Be my A1 French tutor for the three French verb groups. Teach and drill the system: 1st group = -er verbs except aller; 2nd group = -ir verbs whose nous form ends in -issons (finir → nous finissons); 3rd group = everything else, including the -ir verbs that don't make -issons, all -oir and -re verbs, and aller. vocab.phonetic: noo par-LOHN / voo par-LAY / eel PARL

vocab.en: I eat / we eat (keeps the e)
I start / we start (takes a cedilla)

vocab.phonetic: zhuh fee-NEE / tew fee-NEE / eel fee-NEE

vocab.phonetic: noo fee-nee-SOHN / voo fee-nee-SAY / eel fee-NEESS

grammar.point: Two sets of endings — learn them once and they never change

table.title: 1st group: drop -er, add these
table.note: The four highlighted endings are all silent — je parle, tu parles, il parle and ils parlent are pronounced identically. Only nous and vous change the sound.

table2.title: 2nd group: drop -ir, add these
table2.note: The -iss- only appears in the plural. The three singular forms are short — fee-NEE, fee-NEE, fee-NEE — and also sound identical to each other.

grammar.explain: These are the two predictable patterns, and between them they cover the large majority of French verbs. ① 1st group: take the infinitive, drop -er, and add -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent. ② 2nd group: drop -ir and add -is, -is, -it, -issons, -issez, -issent. Both patterns share the same shape — three singular forms that sound alike, then nous in -ons and vous in -ez — so what you're really learning is where the extra -iss- goes. Once these two are automatic, the only verbs left to memorise are the 3rd-group irregulars.

notes.title: Three forms, one sound
notes.body: In both groups the singular forms are pronounced identically: « je parle », « tu parles » and « il parle » are all just « parl », and « je finis », « tu finis », « il finit » are all « fee-NEE ». In speech the pronoun is doing all the work, which is why you can never drop it in French.

notes.title: The -iss- is plural-only
notes.body: This is the shape worth burning in: singular finis, finis, finit — then plural finissons, finissez, finissent. It's also why the « nous » form is the test for the group: the -iss- has nowhere to hide there.

notes.title: Two spelling guards in the 1st group
notes.body: Verbs in -ger keep the e before -ons (nous mangeons, nous voyageons) and verbs in -cer take a cedilla (nous commençons, nous avançons). Without them the g and c would harden into « gons » and « kons » and the word would sound wrong.

notes.title: obéir takes à
notes.body: You obey *to* someone in French: « il n'obéit pas à ses parents ». The verb is a perfectly regular 2nd-group verb — j'obéis, nous obéissons — but the à is not optional, and English speakers drop it constantly. Same shape as répondre à and téléphoner à.

grammar.point: Five irregular verbs — but the endings rhyme more than they look

table.title: être, avoir & aller — the three that build other tenses
table.note: These three carry the rest of the language: être and avoir build the passé composé, and aller builds the near future. Learn them before anything else.

table2.title: faire & prendre
table2.note: je fais, tu fais, il fait all sound the same, and so do the three singular forms of prendre — the difference is only on the page.

grammar.explain: These five carry an enormous share of everyday French, and all five are 3rd group. Look for the pattern rather than memorising thirty-odd forms: nous almost always ends -ons and vous almost always -ez, so the forms worth real attention are the handful that break it — vous êtes, vous faites, ils sont, ils ont, ils font, ils vont. Notice too that the singular forms of faire and prendre are pronounced identically across je, tu and il, so listening won't tell you which one you heard; the sentence around it will. Two pronunciation traps: « nous faisons » is written with ai but spoken « fuh-ZOHN », and aller's nous and vous forms take a liaison — « nous allons » is « noo za-LOHN ».

notes.title: Age uses avoir, not être
notes.body: « J'ai trente ans », literally « I have thirty years ». « Je suis trente ans » is the classic English-speaker error. The same goes for hunger and cold as bodily states: j'ai faim, j'ai froid — but « il fait froid » with faire when you mean the weather.

notes.title: Only three verbs end -es at vous
notes.body: vous êtes, vous faites and vous dites are the whole list — everything else in the language takes vous -ez. Learn those three together and you'll never write « vous faisez ».

notes.title: faire does the weather and the chores
notes.body: French reaches for faire where English uses other verbs: il fait beau (the weather is nice), faire les courses (do the shopping), faire la cuisine (cook), faire du vélo (go cycling). If an activity has no obvious verb, faire is usually the answer.

notes.title: aller has two jobs
notes.body: It means go — « elle va à l'école » — and it also builds the near future when you put an infinitive after it: « je vais manger », I'm going to eat. Exactly like English. It's also the verb that ends in -er and still isn't 1st group, which is why it turns up as the exception in the verb-groups lesson.

notes.title: « être en train de » = right now
notes.body: French has no separate « I am working » form — « je travaille » covers both I work and I am working. When you need to stress that it's happening at this moment, use être en train de + infinitive: « il est en train de travailler », he's in the middle of working. Useful, but don't overuse it — the plain present is normally enough.

examples: Nous sommes en France depuis six mois. (noo SOM ahn FRAHNSS)
Vous êtes prêts ? (voo ZET PREH)
Ils ont deux enfants. (eel ZOHN duh zahn-FAHN)
Qu'est-ce que vous faites ce soir ? (kess kuh voo FET suh SWAHR)
Nous faisons les courses le samedi. (noo fuh-ZOHN lay KOORSS)
Ils prennent le train de huit heures. (eel PREN luh tran)
Nous allons chez nos parents ce week-end. (noo za-LOHN shay noh pa-RAHN)
Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire demain ? (kess kuh tew vah FEHR duh-MAN)
practice: Conjugate être out loud, all six forms, then avoir, then aller.
être or avoir? « Je ___ trente ans » · « Je ___ français » · « J'___ froid » · « Il ___ en retard ».
Fill in: nous ___ (faire) du vélo · vous ___ (faire) la cuisine · ils ___ (prendre) le métro · elle ___ (aller) à l'école.

tutorPrompt: Be my A1 French tutor for the five essential irregular verbs in the present tense: être, avoir, aller, faire and prendre. Drill all six forms of each, then mix them in sentences. Test the traps specifically: age and bodily states take avoir (j'ai trente ans, j'ai faim, j'ai froid) while weather takes faire (il fait froid, il fait beau); vous êtes / vous faites are the -es exceptions, not « vous faisez »; nous faisons is pronounced « fuh-ZOHN » not « feh-ZOHN »; nous allons and vous allez take a liaison, « noo za-LOHN »; and the singular forms of faire and prendre sound identical so I need context. title: Verbs that come with a pronoun — je me lève, tu t'appelles
goal: Conjugate the everyday reflexive verbs in all six persons — including « nous nous levons », which is not a typo — and know why appelle has two l's but appelons has one.

vocab.fr: Je me lève à sept heures.
vocab.phonetic: zhuh muh lev ah set UR

vocab.en: Do you go to bed late?

grammar.point: The pronoun changes with the subject — and nous and vous say it twice

table.title: se lever, all six persons
table.note: The verb is an ordinary -er verb doing nothing unusual — lève, lèves, lève, levons, levez, lèvent. The little pronoun in front is the only new part, and it has to match the subject. For nous and vous the two words happen to be identical, which is why « nous nous levons » looks wrong and is right.

table2.title: s'appeler — count the l's
table2.note: Four forms double the l, two don't — and the sound tells you which. Where you hear « pel », write ll; where you hear a weak « puh », write a single l. It's the same reason se lever grows an accent: « je me lève » (LEV) but « nous nous levons » (luh-VOHN). Nous and vous are the odd ones out in both verbs.

grammar.explain: Some French verbs come with a small pronoun attached, and the dictionary shows it: se lever, s'appeler, se coucher. The pronoun means the action comes back to the subject — se lever is literally to raise oneself — and it changes with the person: me, te, se, nous, vous, se. Three things to get right. ① Before a vowel it elides: je m'appelle, tu t'habilles, il s'appelle. ② The verb itself conjugates completely normally; you're only adding a word in front. ③ Negation wraps around the pair, with ne in front of the little pronoun: « je ne me lève pas », never « je me ne lève pas ». Where English simply says get up, go to bed, hurry, be called, French keeps the pronoun — and leaving it out changes the meaning: « j'appelle Marc » is I'm phoning Marc, « je m'appelle Marc » is my name is Marc.

notes.title: « Nous nous levons » is not a typo
notes.body: Everywhere else the subject and the reflexive pronoun are different words — je/me, tu/te, il/se. For nous and vous they're the same word, so it lands on the page twice in a row: nous nous levons, vous vous couchez, nous nous appelons. Write it twice. Missing one is the single most common mistake with these verbs.

notes.title: The ne goes in front of the pronoun
notes.body: « Je ne me lève pas avant huit heures. » The ne comes before me, not before the verb, because the pronoun and the verb are treated as one block. Same everywhere: « il ne se couche pas tard », « nous ne nous dépêchons pas ». The rest of the negation frame — ne… plus, ne… jamais — behaves exactly the same way.

notes.title: Drop the pronoun and you change the verb
notes.body: « Il appelle sa mère » is he's phoning his mother. « Il s'appelle Marc » is his name is Marc. Same for lever: « je lève la main » is I raise my hand, « je me lève » is I get up. The pronoun is not decoration — it's what tells you the action lands back on the subject.

notes.title: In an order, the pronoun moves behind
notes.body: « Dépêche-toi ! », « Assieds-toi ! », « Asseyez-vous ! », « Reposez-vous bien ! » — after the verb, joined by a hyphen, and te turns into toi. You'll hear these long before you learn the imperative properly, so learn them as fixed phrases now.

examples: Le matin, je me réveille à six heures et je me lève à sept heures. (zhuh muh ray-VEY … zhuh muh LEV)
— Comment tu t'appelles ? — Je m'appelle Ekta. (koh-mahn tew ta-PEL)
Nous nous levons tôt, même le dimanche. (noo noo luh-VOHN toh, mem luh dee-MAHNSH)
Ils s'appellent Marc et Julie, et ils habitent à Lyon. (eel sa-PEL mark ay zhew-LEE)
Je ne me couche pas avant minuit. (zhuh nuh muh koosh pah ah-vahn mee-NWEE)
Dépêche-toi, on va être en retard ! (day-pesh TWAH, ohn va eh-truh ahn ruh-TAR)
practice: Say se coucher through all six persons out loud, then se dépêcher.
Describe your morning in three steps: je me réveille… je me lève… je m'habille…
Fill the doubles: « nous ___ levons à six heures » · « vous ___ couchez tard ».
How many l's? « nous nous appel___ons » · « ils s'appel___ent » · « je m'appel___e ».
Make it negative: « je me lève tôt » → ___ · « il se dépêche » → ___ .
Two orders: tell a friend to hurry (___-toi !), then a room of people to sit down (___-vous !).
Same verb, two meanings: say « I'm phoning Julie » and « my name is Julie ».
tutorPrompt: Be my A1 French tutor for reflexive verbs (les verbes pronominaux). Drill se lever, se coucher, se réveiller, s'habiller, se dépêcher, se reposer and s'appeler through all six persons. Push hard on the two things I get wrong: the doubled nous and vous forms (« nous nous levons », « vous vous appelez ») where the word appears twice, and the spelling of s'appeler — two l's for m'appelle, t'appelles, s'appelle and s'appellent, one l for nous appelons and vous appelez. Ask me about my daily routine one question at a time so the verbs come out naturally, and throw in the imperative forms « Dépêche-toi ! » and « Asseyez-vous ! ». Correct every attempt and end with what I still need to review.

title: The past tense — passé composé with avoir
goal: Talk about what you did — how the passé composé is built with avoir, and the four jobs French gives it.

grammar.point: avoir (present) + past participle

table.title: two pieces, and only the first one is conjugated
table.note: The participle never changes with avoir — mangé for everyone, whoever is speaking. Only the auxiliary moves. (Agreement does exist with avoir, but only when the object comes first, which is a B1 problem.) In the negative the ne… pas wraps the auxiliary alone: « je n'ai pas mangé », never « je n'ai mangé pas ».

table2.title: the four jobs it does

rows.label: a finished action, pinned to a moment
a chain of actions in a story
cells: Je suis rentré, j'ai mangé et je me suis couché.

rows.label: a past act still felt now
cells: J'ai cassé mon téléphone. — et il l'est toujours.

highlight: J'ai cassé mon téléphone. — et il l'est toujours.
table2.note: What unites all four: the action is over and it has edges. That's the whole contrast with the imparfait, which describes a past with no edges — what things were like, what you used to do. That tense comes at B1; until then, if it happened and it finished, use this one.

grammar.explain: The passé composé does the work of two English tenses at once: « j'ai mangé » is both I ate and I have eaten, and French never distinguishes them. It is built from avoir in the present plus a past participle — and avoir covers almost every verb, the exception being the movement verbs that take être, which have their own lesson. The participle follows a rule for the first two groups: -er verbs give -é (parler → parlé, manger → mangé), -ir verbs that go -issons give -i (finir → fini). The third group has no rule and has to be learnt — fait, vu, pris, dit, eu, été to begin with, and the full working list in the lesson that follows this one. Two mechanics to get right from day one. Negation clamps around the auxiliary only: je n'ai pas compris. And the question keeps the two pieces welded together: « Qu'est-ce que tu as fait ? », « Tu as mangé ? », « As-tu compris ? ».

examples: Hier, j'ai mangé au restaurant et j'ai vu un film. (ee-YEHR, zhay mahn-ZHAY oh res-toh-RAHN ay zhay vew uhn FEELM)
— Qu'est-ce que tu as fait ce week-end ? — J'ai travaillé. (kess-kuh tew ah feh suh week-END ? zhay tra-va-YAY)
practice: Say three things you did yesterday using « j'ai… ».
Form the passé composé of: parler, manger, regarder, finir, choisir.
Put it in the negative: « J'ai compris » → ___ . (mind where pas goes)
Slide the adverb in: « J'ai mangé » + déjà → ___ .
Ask « Qu'est-ce que tu as fait hier ? » and then answer it in three sentences.
Which job is this doing? — « J'ai perdu mes clés. »
tutorPrompt: Be my A2 French tutor focused on the passé composé with avoir. Ask me what I did yesterday and last weekend, one question at a time, in simple French. Gently correct my past participles and my use of avoir. After about eight exchanges, list the participles I should memorise.

notes.title: « Déjà » and « jamais » go inside, not after
notes.body: Short adverbs slide between the auxiliary and the participle: « j'ai déjà mangé », « je n'ai jamais vu ce film », « il a beaucoup travaillé », « tu as bien dormi ? ». Longer ones stay outside: « j'ai travaillé sérieusement ». Getting déjà into the middle is one of the fastest ways to stop sounding like a beginner.

notes.title: The tense is called « composé » because it has two parts
notes.body: Un temps composé is any tense built from an auxiliary plus a participle — passé composé, plus-que-parfait, futur antérieur. Un temps simple is one word: je mange, je mangeais, je mangerai. Once you see the split, half of French grammar sorts itself: learn the auxiliaries once and every compound tense becomes the same trick at a different setting.

notes.title: Which auxiliary? Almost always avoir
notes.body: Avoir takes everything except a short list of movement and change-of-state verbs (aller, venir, partir, arriver, entrer, sortir, monter, descendre, rester, naître, mourir, tomber, passer, retourner) and every reflexive verb — « je me suis levé ». Those are the next lesson. If a verb isn't on that list, it takes avoir, and that includes verbs that feel like movement: j'ai marché, j'ai couru, j'ai voyagé, j'ai nagé.

title: The past participles — two you can predict, twenty you can't
goal: Build the past participle of any verb: the two endings that follow a rule, and the short irregular list that carries most French conversation.

vocab.en: I put / I put on — mettre

grammar.point: Three groups, three endings — and then the list

table.title: the part that follows a rule

rows.label: 3e — everything else
cells: voir → vu · dormir → dormi · prendre → pris · dire → dit

table.note: The first two rows are watertight, and they cover the great majority of verbs — every new verb French invents joins the first group. The third row isn't a rule, it's a warning: those endings exist, but which one a verb takes has to be learnt one verb at a time.

table2.title: the third group, worth learning as a block
table2.note: Eight rows, about twenty verbs — and they are the twenty that come up most. Notice they cluster: a whole family in -u (pu, voulu, dû, vu, reçu, bu, lu, perdu, répondu), a small family in -is / -it (mis, pris, dit, écrit), and a stubborn family in -ert (ouvert, offert, découvert). Learn the clusters, not twenty separate facts.

grammar.explain: A passé composé is two pieces: an auxiliary in the present, and a past participle. The auxiliary is the easy half — avoir for almost everything, être for the movement verbs. The participle is where the work is. For groups 1 and 2 it is pure arithmetic: cut the -er and add -é, cut the -ir and add -i. Group 3 — the verbs that were already irregular in the present — keeps being irregular here, and there's no derivation to fall back on: you learn them. The good news is how small the list is and how it clumps. Once you know prendre → pris, you get comprendre → compris, apprendre → appris, surprendre → surpris for free, because compounds always follow their parent verb. Same for ouvrir → ouvert giving you couvrir → couvert, découvrir → découvert, offrir → offert, souffrir → souffert. Learn eight patterns and you've covered several dozen verbs. One caution while you drill: a participle is not a conjugated verb. « J'ai pris » is a sentence; « pris » on its own is not. Always practise it welded to its auxiliary.

notes.title: « eu » is two letters and one sound
notes.body: Avoir's participle is written eu and pronounced like the u in « tu » — « ew ». « J'ai eu » comes out « zhay EW », with the e doing nothing at all. It looks like it should be two syllables and it isn't. Same trick inside « il a eu », « nous avons eu ».

notes.title: dû keeps its accent only in the masculine singular
notes.body: The circumflex on dû exists for one reason: to stop it being confused with « du », the partitive. That job disappears the moment the word changes shape, so the accent goes with it — dû, but due, dus, dues. Nobody would misread « elle a été due » as « some ».

notes.title: The -ert family are not -ir verbs
notes.body: Ouvrir, offrir, couvrir, découvrir, souffrir end in -ir and behave like nothing else: their present tense takes -er endings (j'ouvre, tu ouvres) and their participle ends in -ert. Five verbs, one exception, and « j'ai ouvert la porte » is a sentence you'll say weekly.

notes.title: reçu keeps the cedilla for a reason
notes.body: Without the ç, « recu » would be read « ruh-KEW » — a c before u is hard. The cedilla holds the s sound: reçu, « ruh-SEW ». Same logic behind ça, français, garçon, and behind « nous commençons » growing a cedilla the present tense doesn't otherwise need.

notes.title: Vouloir, pouvoir and devoir in the past mean something sharper
notes.body: In the passé composé these three stop being vague. « J'ai voulu » is I decided to, I tried to — not I wanted. « J'ai pu » is I managed to. « J'ai dû » is either I had to, or I must have: « il a dû partir » is both « he had to leave » and « he must have left », and only the context separates them. Say « je voulais » (imparfait) if you mean the softer I wanted.

notes.title: The participle you already learnt as an adjective
notes.body: Past participles moonlight as adjectives all over French: une porte ouverte, un plat fait maison, du vin bu, une lettre écrite. If you can already say « fermé » on a shop door, you already know a participle. The passé composé is just that word with an auxiliary bolted in front of it.

examples: J'ai pris le métro et j'ai lu tout le trajet. (zhay pree luh may-TROH ay zhay lew too luh tra-ZHAY)
Je n'ai pas compris la question, pouvez-vous répéter ? (zhuh nay pa kohn-PREE lah kess-TYOHN)
Elle m'a écrit hier, mais je n'ai pas encore répondu. (el ma ay-KREE ee-YEHR)
On a bu un café et on a beaucoup parlé. (ohn na bew uhn ka-FAY)
J'ai dû partir avant la fin. (zhay dew par-TEER a-vahn lah FAN)
J'ai reçu ta lettre, merci ! (zhay ruh-SEW tah LET-ruh)
Ils ont ouvert le magasin à neuf heures. (eel zohn oo-VEHR luh ma-ga-ZAN)
Qu'est-ce que tu as fait ? — J'ai eu une longue journée. (zhay ew ewn lohng zhoor-NAY)
practice: Give the participle: parler · finir · choisir · regarder · grandir.
Now the ones with no rule: prendre · dire · voir · boire · devoir · ouvrir.
Fill the family: prendre → pris, so comprendre → ___ , apprendre → ___ , surprendre → ___ .

Careful: how do you say « I had a good day »? (the auxiliary and the participle are the same verb)
Spot the wrong one: j'ai prendu · j'ai mis · j'ai voulu · j'ai écrivé.
tutorPrompt: Be my A2 French tutor drilling past participles. Give me infinitives one at a time and have me answer with « j'ai + participle » — never the bare participle. Mix in the predictable -er and -ir verbs so I stay fast on those, then hammer the irregular list: mis, pris, compris, appris, dit, écrit, pu, voulu, dû, vu, reçu, bu, lu, perdu, répondu, ouvert, offert, découvert, dormi, eu, fait, été. When I invent one (j'ai prendu, j'ai écrivé), tell me the real one and the family it belongs to. Then ask me eight questions about my week so I have to produce them in real sentences. Finish with the ten I should write on a card.

title: Past tense with être & getting around
goal: Say where you went, came from and stayed — the verbs that take être, and the agreement that comes with them.

vocab.fr: en train / en bus / en voiture
vocab.phonetic: ahn TRAN / ahn BEWSS / ahn vwah-TEWR
vocab.en: by train / by bus / by car

grammar.point: The être verbs travel in opposite pairs — and the participle agrees

table.title: learn them two at a time
table.note: Fourteen verbs, seven pairs, and every one of them is either a movement or an arrival into a state. Their compounds come along too: revenir, devenir, rentrer, remonter, repartir. Everything else in French takes avoir.

table2.title: with être, the participle behaves like an adjective
table2.note: Almost all of it is silent: allé, allée, allés, allées are four spellings of one sound. You'll only ever hear the agreement on participles ending in a consonant — morte, and at B1 the ones like « prise » and « offerte ». Which means this rule costs you nothing when speaking and everything when writing.

grammar.explain: A short, closed list of verbs refuses avoir and takes être instead: the ones on the left, all about going somewhere or changing state. « Je suis allé au marché », « elle est née à Paris », « nous sommes restés deux jours ». And because they take être, the participle agrees with the subject exactly like an adjective — add -e for feminine, -s for plural, -es for both: je suis allée (a woman speaking), nous sommes allés, elles sont arrivées. Reflexive verbs join the same club: se lever, se coucher, s'appeler all take être — « je me suis levé(e) à sept heures ». The trap to know about now, because you will meet it within a week: six of these verbs — monter, descendre, sortir, rentrer, passer, retourner — switch back to avoir the moment they take a direct object. « Je suis sorti » is I went out; « j'ai sorti la poubelle » is I took the bin out. « Elle est montée » is she went up; « elle a monté les valises » is she carried the cases up. Nothing goes wrong if you don't use them transitively — but you need to recognise it when you hear it.

examples: Le week-end dernier, je suis allé(e) à Lyon en train. (luh week-end dehr-NYAY, zhuh swee a-LAY ah lee-OHN ahn TRAN)
Elle est née à Paris et elle est restée en France. (el eh nay ah pa-REE ay el eh res-TAY ahn FRAHNSS)
Nous sommes arrivés il y a huit mois. (noo som za-ree-VAY eel ee ah wee MWAH)
Ils sont partis tôt et ils sont revenus tard. (eel sohn par-TEE toh ay eel sohn ruh-vuh-NEW TAR)
Je suis tombé dans l'escalier. (zhuh swee tohn-BAY dahn les-ka-LYAY)
Je suis sorti à huit heures — mais j'ai sorti le chien avant. (zhuh swee sor-TEE … zhay sor-TEE luh SHYAN)
Je me suis levé(e) à six heures ce matin. (zhuh muh swee luh-VAY ah see ZUR)

Give the seven pairs back from memory: arriver / ___ , aller / ___ , entrer / ___ …
Add the right ending for a woman speaking: allé · venu · parti · resté.
Être or avoir? — marcher · sortir · voyager · descendre · rester · courir.
Explain the difference: « je suis passé chez toi » / « j'ai passé deux heures chez toi ».
Put a reflexive in the past: « je me lève à sept heures » → hier, ___ .

tutorPrompt: Be my A2 French tutor on the passé composé with être. First check I know the closed list — the seven opposite pairs plus their compounds and all reflexives — by asking me « être ou avoir ? » for a mix of verbs, including tempting ones like marcher, voyager and courir that take avoir. Then ask me where I went recently, how I got there and what time I got up, one question at a time. Correct my auxiliary choice first and my agreement second (-e for feminine, -s for plural). notes.title: Six of them go both ways
notes.body: Monter, descendre, sortir, rentrer, passer and retourner take être when nothing follows them and avoir when a direct object does. « Je suis passé chez toi » (I dropped by) versus « j'ai passé deux heures chez toi » (I spent two hours). The meaning shifts with the auxiliary, which is why French keeps both.
