Say something to me, then have me report it accurately — shifting tenses (présent → imparfait, futur → conditionnel, passé composé → plus-que-parfait), pronouns and time words. Cover statements, questions and commands. Correct my tense shifts with a one-line why, and finish with the present → past shift table.

title: The news & the passive voice
goal: Follow and discuss the news, and use the passive voice the way the French press does.

vocab.fr: il paraît que / on dit que
vocab.phonetic: eel pah-reh KUH / ohn dee KUH

grammar.point: La voix passive

table.note: être carries the tense; the participle agrees with the subject. Name the doer with « par ». When the doer is vague, French prefers active « on »: « on a annoncé une réforme ».

grammar.explain: The passive puts the receiver of the action first — common in news and formal writing. Form: être (in the right tense) + past participle, agreeing with the subject (grid): « une loi a été votée », « le suspect sera interrogé ». Name the doer with « par ».

examples: Une réforme du système de santé a été annoncée hier par le gouvernement. (ewn ray-FORM dew sees-tem duh sahn-TAY ah ay-tay ah-nohn-SAY ee-YEHR par luh goo-vehr-nuh-MAHN)
Selon une étude, le prix des loyers a augmenté de 5 % en un an. (suh-lohn ewn ay-TEWD, luh pree day lwah-YAY ah ohg-mahn-TAY duh sank poor-SAHN ahn nuhn AHN)
practice: Turn an active sentence into the passive: « Le maire a inauguré le pont » → « Le pont… ».
Report a statistic with « selon une étude, … ».
Use « on » to stay impersonal: « On a annoncé que… ».
Summarise a headline you saw this week in one French sentence.
tutorPrompt: Be my B2 French tutor for the news and the passive voice. Give me short French headlines or facts and have me (1) rephrase them in the passive (être + participe passé, with agreement) and (2) discuss them. Also drill the active « on » alternative and reporting with « selon ». Correct my participle agreement and register, and end with ten useful news/press words.

title: Debating big issues — lequel, auquel, duquel
goal: Discuss society and the environment, and connect complex ideas precisely with lequel, auquel and duquel.

grammar.point: Les pronoms relatifs composés : lequel, auquel, duquel

table.note: Use after a preposition (pour lequel, avec lesquelles). à and de contract just like the articles. Shortcut: for a person, « qui » works — « la personne avec qui je parle ».

grammar.explain: After a preposition (pour, avec, sans, grâce à…), the relative pronoun becomes lequel and agrees with its noun — see grid. With à and de it contracts exactly like the articles (à + lequel = auquel, de + lequel = duquel).

examples: Le réchauffement climatique est un enjeu auquel nous devons tous réfléchir. (luh ray-shoh-fuh-mahn klee-mah-teek eh tuhn ahn-ZHUH oh-kel noo duh-vohn toos ray-flay-SHEER)
Voici les raisons pour lesquelles je soutiens cette réforme. (vwah-see lay reh-ZOHN poor lay-KEL zhuh soo-tyan set ray-FORM)
practice: Complete with the right form: « C'est un sujet ___ je m'intéresse » (à → auquel).
Give « les raisons pour lesquelles… » you support or oppose an idea.
Make a sentence with « grâce auquel / à laquelle ».
State an environmental enjeu and one way to « lutter contre » it.

Pick an issue (climate, inequality, globalisation) and debate it with me, pushing me to link ideas with lequel, auquel and duquel (and « pour lesquelles », « grâce auquel »). Correct the contractions and agreement, and finish with five « pour lesquelles… »-type phrases plus key vocabulary for the topic.

title: Formal writing — letters & complaints
goal: Write a clear formal letter or email — a request, a complaint, an application — with the right register and set phrases.

vocab.fr: Je me permets de vous écrire
vocab.phonetic: zhuh muh pehr-meh duh voo zay-KREER

vocab.en: I am writing in order to
I would be grateful if you would

vocab.fr: Je vous prie d'agréer mes salutations distinguées
vocab.phonetic: zhuh voo pree dah-gray-AY may sah-lew-tah-syohn dees-tan-GAY

grammar.point: Le registre formel & le gérondif

table.note: Set phrases: « je me permets de… », « je vous serais reconnaissant de… ». Plus the gérondif (en + -ant): « en attendant votre réponse ».

grammar.explain: Formal French uses vous, avoids slang, and leans on set phrases and precise verbs — see the register grid. A useful tool is the gérondif (« en » + present participle, the nous-stem + -ant) for how/why/when with the same subject: « en attendant votre réponse », « j'ai appris le français en travaillant ».

examples: Je me permets de vous écrire afin de solliciter un rendez-vous. (zhuh muh pehr-meh duh voo zay-kree ah-fan duh soh-lee-see-TAY uhn rahn-day-VOO)
En attendant votre réponse, je vous prie d'agréer mes salutations distinguées. (ahn nah-tahn-dahn voh-truh ray-PONS, zhuh voo pree dah-gray-AY may sah-lew-tah-syohn dees-tan-GAY)

title: The DELF B2 oral exam
goal: Walk into the DELF B2 oral ready — present a viewpoint from a short text, structure it, and defend it in the debate.

vocab.fr: le document soulève la question de
vocab.phonetic: luh doh-kew-mahn soo-lev lah kes-tyohn DUH
vocab.en: the text raises the question of
I'll cover it in two parts
first of all / then / to finish

grammar.point: Présenter et défendre un point de vue
grammar.explain: The B2 oral has two stages: a monologue presenting a viewpoint on a short document, then a debate with the examiner. Structure the monologue: introduce the document (« Ce document, tiré de…, traite de… / soulève la question de… »), announce your plan (« Je l'aborderai en deux parties »), develop with connectors (« tout d'abord », « par ailleurs », « en revanche »), and conclude (« en somme, … »). In the debate, defend your view but stay flexible: agree-then-qualify (« vous avez raison, cependant… »), nuance (« cela dépend de… », « dans une certaine mesure ») and back claims with examples (« par exemple », « concrètement »).

examples: Ce document soulève la question de la place des écrans dans l'éducation ; je l'aborderai en deux parties. (suh doh-kew-mahn soo-lev lah kes-tyohn duh lah plass day zay-KRAN dahn lay-dew-kah-SYOHN ; zhuh lah-bor-duh-ray ahn duh par-TEE)
Vous avez raison sur ce point, cependant il ne faut pas négliger les risques. (voo zah-vay reh-zohn sewr suh PWAN, suh-pahn-dahn eel nuh foh pah nay-glee-ZHAY lay REESK)
practice: Introduce a document: « Ce document traite de… et soulève la question de… ».
Announce a two-part plan and give your thesis.
Agree, then qualify in a debate: « Vous avez raison, cependant… ».
Give a 60-second spoken opinion on screen time, then defend it against one objection.
tutorPrompt: Act as a DELF B2 oral examiner. Give me a short French text or statement on a societal topic; I'll take a minute, then present a structured viewpoint (introduce the document, announce a plan, develop with connectors, conclude). Then debate me with two or three challenging follow-ups and make me defend and nuance my position. Stay in French at B2, and at the end score me on the DELF oral grid (clarity, structure, argument, range, accuracy) with three concrete fixes.

title: L'outre-mer — les mêmes droits partout ?
goal: Answer the class debate question — are rights as well respected outre-mer as in mainland France? — with the two structures it takes, and the constitutional ground the answer stands on.

figures.alt: A world map of the French overseas territories. In the Atlantic: Guadeloupe, Martinique and Guyane under article 73, Saint-Martin, Saint-Barthélemy and Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon under article 74. In the Indian Ocean: Mayotte and La Réunion under article 73. In the Pacific, which wraps round both edges of the map: Wallis-et-Futuna and la Polynésie française under article 74, and la Nouvelle-Calédonie under title XIII of the Constitution. Mainland France is marked in Europe, with la Corse flagged separately as not outre-mer. Below, three distance bars from Paris: 6 700 km to Pointe-à-Pitre, 9 350 km to Saint-Denis de La Réunion, 15 700 km to Papeete.
figures.caption: Same Republic, same Constitution, three oceans. The colour is the legal status: article 73 takes French law directly, article 74 has a statute of its own. La Corse is on the map precisely to show it is not on that list.

figures.alt: A schematic of where the 1905 law of separation does not apply. Mainland France is drawn as a stylised hexagon under the 1905 law, with one amber area at its north-east corner: Alsace-Moselle, German in 1905 and still under the Concordat of 1801, where the state pays priests, pastors and rabbis and religion is taught in public schools. La Corse sits below the hexagon, under the 1905 law. A separate amber box 7 000 km away shows Guyane in South America, where an 1828 royal ordinance still stands and the collectivité pays the Catholic clergy.
figures.caption: The 1905 law is the rule everywhere except the two amber patches — one in the Hexagone, one outre-mer. Whichever side of the debate you argue, this is the fact worth having ready.

grammar.point: Saying « as … as » — and what changes the moment you disagree

table.title: French splits « as … as » three ways
table.note: Aussi goes with words, autant with amounts. The one bridge is de: autant de moyens, never « aussi de moyens ».

table2.title: « Je pense que… » — until you disagree

rows.label: c'est sûr
cells: indicatif — qu'il y a un problème

rows.label: c'est possible
cells: subjonctif — qu'il y ait un problème

highlight: subjonctif — qu'il y ait un problème
table2.note: It isn't about how much doubt is in your head — it's about whether the sentence still asserts the thing. Two forms cover most of it: être → soient, avoir → ait.

grammar.explain: The class question is built from both tables at once. « Les droits sont-ils autant respectés outre-mer qu'en métropole ? » needs the first one: French puts aussi in front of an adjective or an adverb, autant after a verb, and autant de in front of a noun. English makes none of those distinctions, which is why « aussi de moyens » is the slip an examiner hears first. Answering it needs the second: je pense que asserts something, so it takes the indicative — negate it and the sentence stops asserting, so it flips to the subjunctive. Je ne pense pas que les droits soient respectés. That flip is the most visible B2 marker you have, because it fires the moment you disagree.

notes.title: L'outre-mer is two categories — and la Corse is in neither
notes.body: The map above is the note. Article 73 means French law applies directly; article 74 means a statute of its own. La Corse is on neither list — it sits inside metropolitan France with a special status, so its autonomy debate rests on different ground.

notes.title: Article premier — learn the sentence
notes.body: « La France est une République indivisible, laïque, démocratique et sociale. Elle assure l'égalité devant la loi de tous les citoyens sans distinction d'origine, de race ou de religion. » Quotable in the DELF oral, and it comes up in the naturalisation interview. It also hands you both sides of the debate at once.

notes.title: La croix dans l’espace public — la règle de 1905
notes.body: La laïcité, in practice. The 1905 law forbids new religious signs on public land; anything older is left alone, which is why every village church keeps its cross. Put up a new one and it becomes a case for the tribunal administratif — Ploërmel, 2017, where the Conseil d'État let the statue stay and took the cross down. The two places the law never reached are in the second figure above.

examples: La Réunion est souvent citée comme un modèle de vivre-ensemble. (lah ray-ew-NYOHN)
Dans la même rue, on peut trouver une église, un temple tamoul et une mosquée. (uhn TAHMPL ta-MOOL)
Une croix installée sur un terrain communal peut être contestée devant le tribunal administratif. (ewn KRWAH ann-sta-LAY)
Je ne pense pas que les droits soient aussi bien respectés qu'en métropole. (kuh lay drwah SWAHN)
Les services publics sont-ils aussi efficaces outre-mer que dans l'Hexagone ? (oh-SEE ay-fee-KASS)
practice: Fill the gap with aussi · autant · autant de: « Il n'y a pas ___ investissements qu'en métropole. » · « L'eau n'est pas ___ fiable qu'ici. » · « On n'en parle pas ___ que des sujets métropolitains. »
Say the same opinion twice — once with « Je pense que… », once with « Je ne pense pas que… » — and change the verb.
Answer the class question out loud in ninety seconds, using article premier and the two exceptions to the 1905 law.
Article 73, article 74, or neither? — la Guadeloupe · la Polynésie française · la Corse · La Réunion.
Explain « la laïcité » to an English-speaking friend, in French, in three sentences — without using the word « secular ».
Build the DELF shape: « D'un côté… », « D'un autre côté… », « En fin de compte… » — one paragraph each.
tutorPrompt: Act as a DELF B2 oral examiner, in French throughout. Put this question to me: « Est-ce que vous pensez que les droits sont autant respectés dans les régions d'outre-mer qu'en France métropolitaine ? » Give me a minute to prepare, then make me answer in the DELF shape — introduction, plan annoncé, deux arguments avec exemples, conclusion — and push back three times. Draw on the real material: l'article premier, la différence entre l'article 73 et l'article 74, la croix dans l'espace public et la loi de 1905, et le fait que cette loi ne s'applique ni en Alsace-Moselle ni en Guyane. Correct exactly two things per turn: the comparison structures (aussi + adjectif/adverbe, autant + verbe, autant de + nom, never « aussi de »), and the subjunctive after « je ne pense pas que » — soient, ait, puisse. Finish with a DELF grid score and three concrete fixes.

title: L'histoire — de l'esclavage à la départementalisation
goal: How the overseas territories became French — three centuries in three stages — and the tense you need to read any of it: le passé simple.

figures.alt: A three-band timeline. First band, l'esclavage, 1635 to 1848: in 1685 the Code Noir regulates the status of enslaved people; in 1794 the Convention abolishes slavery; in 1802 Napoléon restores it, cancelling the abolition; on 27 April 1848 the décret Schœlcher abolishes it for good. Second band, l'engagisme, 1848 to 1946: the plantations bring in indentured workers, mostly from India, which is the origin of the Tamil temples of La Réunion. Third band, les départements, 1946 to today: the four old colonies become French départements under the « loi d'assimilation », with Aimé Césaire as its rapporteur; from 1963 the BUMIDOM organises departure for mainland France; in 2001 the loi Taubira recognises slavery as a crime against humanity.
figures.caption: Read the middle band and the Tamil temples of lesson two stop being a curiosity — they are the direct consequence of what replaced slavery. And read the bottom one before you judge 1946: becoming a département was a demand for equality, made by the territories themselves.

grammar.point: Le passé simple — the tense you read but never speak

table.title: reconnaître le passé simple, et le rendre en passé composé
table.note: Two forms carry most history writing: fut and eut. Note the trap on the -ir verbs — « il abolit » is identical in the present and the passé simple, and only the surrounding dates tell you which one you are reading.

table2.title: Sept dates, toutes au passé simple

cells: le Code Noir régla le statut des esclaves
the Code Noir sets the rules
le décret Schœlcher l’abolit pour de bon

highlight: le décret Schœlcher l’abolit pour de bon
table2.note: Every verb in the middle column is a passé simple, which is exactly how you will meet this timeline in a textbook or on a museum panel. Say the same seven lines in the passé composé and you have the spoken version: Napoléon l’a rétabli, le décret l’a aboli, elles sont devenues des départements.

grammar.explain: French keeps a separate tense for written narrative, and at B2 you read it rather than produce it. Le passé simple is what you meet in history books, museum captions and novels, while speech uses the passé composé for the very same events: « Napoléon rétablit l'esclavage » on the panel, « Napoléon a rétabli l'esclavage » in the café. The endings are regular enough — parler gives il parla, ils parlèrent — but the forms you actually need are the irregular ones, above all être and avoir: il fut, ils furent, il eut, ils eurent. Recognise those four and most historical prose opens up. One real ambiguity: for -ir verbs the third person singular is identical in the present, so « il abolit » is only datable from context.

notes.title: Why there are two — le passé simple is the original
notes.body: Le passé simple is the older tense, inherited from Latin, and for centuries it was simply the past. Le passé composé began as something else: « j'ai écrit la lettre » once meant « I have the letter written ». It crept into speech, took the job over entirely and never gave it back — while writing kept the old one. Two forms, one meaning, split by medium, and English has no equivalent.

notes.title: Two abolitions, not one
notes.body: The Convention abolished slavery in 1794, but it was never applied everywhere — La Réunion refused it outright, and Martinique was under British occupation. Napoléon restored it in 1802, and Guadeloupe rose against the restoration under Louis Delgrès, who died at Matouba rather than submit. Only the décret of 27 April 1848, carried by Victor Schœlcher, ended it for good. That is why the date is a reversal and not a straight line.

notes.title: L'engagisme — why La Réunion has Tamil temples
notes.body: Abolition did not end the plantations' hunger for labour, so from 1848 the colonies brought in travailleurs engagés on long contracts, above all from southern India. Those families are the direct origin of the Tamil community you met in the Réunion lesson — the temples, Dipavali, the surnames. Knowing this is what separates a description of le vivre-ensemble from an explanation of it.

notes.title: 1946 — the territories asked for it
notes.body: The law of 19 March 1946 was known as the loi d'assimilation, and it was pushed by the colonies' own elected representatives. Aimé Césaire, deputy for Martinique and one of the great poets of the century, was its rapporteur. Becoming a département was a demand for equality, not something done to them — which is exactly the promise that the question « are the rights the same everywhere? » measures against.

notes.title: Le BUMIDOM — a migration the State organised
notes.body: From 1963 to the early 1980s a state body, the Bureau pour le développement des migrations, arranged departures from the DOM to fill labour shortages in mainland France. Tens of thousands went through it directly, far more followed on their own. It is remembered unevenly — as opportunity by some, as an organised drain by others — and the argument is still live.

examples: En 1685, le Code Noir régla le statut des esclaves dans les colonies. (luh kod NWAHR)
La Convention abolit l'esclavage en 1794, mais Napoléon le rétablit en 1802. (nah-po-lay-OHN luh ray-ta-BLEE)
Le décret du 27 avril 1848 abolit l'esclavage pour de bon. (dew vangt-set a-VREEL)
Après l'abolition, l'engagisme fit venir des travailleurs indiens. (lahn-ga-ZEESM fee vuh-NEER)
En 1946, les quatre vieilles colonies devinrent des départements français. (duh-VANR day day-par-tuh-MAHN)
Aujourd'hui on dirait plutôt : Napoléon a rétabli l'esclavage. (a ray-ta-BLEE)
practice: Put these into the passé composé: il fut · elle devint · ils abolirent · il fit · elle prit · ils organisèrent.
Read the seven dates aloud, then tell the same story again in the passé composé.
Which year? — le Code Noir · la première abolition · le rétablissement · le décret Schœlcher · la départementalisation.
Explain « l'engagisme » in French in three sentences, and say what it has to do with the temples of La Réunion.
Spot the trap: « il finit », « il abolit » — present or passé simple? What tells you?
Answer out loud in two minutes: « La départementalisation de 1946 a-t-elle tenu ses promesses ? »
tutorPrompt: Act as a French history tutor at B2, in French throughout. The subject is how the outre-mer became French: le Code Noir in 1685, the abolition of 1794 that was never fully applied, its rétablissement by Napoléon in 1802 and the revolt of Louis Delgrès at Matouba, the décret Schœlcher of 27 April 1848, l'engagisme that brought indentured workers from India and created the Tamil community of La Réunion, the loi de départementalisation of 19 March 1946 with Aimé Césaire as rapporteur, the BUMIDOM from 1963, and the loi Taubira of 2001. First give me a short written paragraph in the passé simple and make me translate it into the spoken passé composé. Then question me on the chronology, and finish by making me argue whether 1946 kept its promise. Correct exactly two things per turn: my passé simple recognition — especially fut, furent, eut, eurent, devint, devinrent — and my dates. End with three concrete fixes and the phrases I hesitated on.

title: La Réunion & la Corse — deux îles, deux laïcités
goal: Contrast two French islands — one where four religions share a calendar, one that went to court over a cross — and learn the connectors that make a comparison sound B2.

figures.alt: A side-by-side comparison of two French islands. On the left, La Réunion in the Indian Ocean, about 880 000 inhabitants: four communities share the island — Catholics, Tamil Hindus, Muslims, and Buddhists and Chinese — and Dipavali, l'Aïd, Noël and the Chinese New Year are all publicly marked; mixed marriages are ordinary. On the right, la Corse in the Mediterranean, about 350 000 inhabitants: one largely Catholic tradition, with confréries and processions, and the cross as a marker of identity. Below it, the Quasquara case in three dates: 2022, the council erects a cross; 2025, the tribunal administratif de Bastia overturns the mayor's refusal to remove it; 2026, the cour administrative d'appel de Marseille confirms the removal.
figures.caption: Four colours on the left, one on the right — that is the whole lesson in a glance. Same Republic and same 1905 law, but La Réunion's question is how four religions share a public calendar, and la Corse's is whether a cross can be cultural rather than religious.

vocab.en: to coexist, to live side by side

grammar.point: Opposing two things — and the one connector that takes the subjunctive

table.title: les connecteurs de l’opposition et de la concession

rows.label: alors que · tandis que
cells: alors qu’ici on défend un héritage

rows.label: bien que · quoique
cells: bien que la croix soit ancienne…

rows.label: même si
cells: même si la croix est ancienne…

table.note: These two look interchangeable in English — both come out as « although » — and they are not. Bien que takes the subjunctive, même si never does. If you only remember one thing from this lesson, remember that pair.

table2.title: L’affaire de Quasquara — comment une affaire avance

rows.label: ① 2022
cells: the council puts up a cross

rows.label: ②
cells: a resident asks for it to be removed

rows.label: ⑥ 2026
cells: la cour d’appel confirme le retrait
the appeal court upholds the removal

table2.note: Step ⑤ is the one worth noticing: the court does not order the cross down, it annuls the mayor’s refusal to take it down. French administrative law works on the decision, not the object — which is why you attack un refus, not une croix.

grammar.explain: A comparison is only as good as the words joining its halves, and French sorts them by what comes next. Alors que and tandis que take a full clause in the indicative and are the workhorses of a contrast. Contrairement à takes a noun, so it needs a person or a place after it, never a verb. En revanche, pourtant and cependant simply sit inside a sentence and need nothing special. Then there is the pair that catches everyone: bien que and même si both translate as « although », but bien que takes the subjunctive — bien que la croix soit ancienne — while même si takes the indicative and never wavers. English gives you no warning, so it has to be learned as a fact about the two words rather than a rule you can reason out.

notes.title: Bien que + subjonctif, même si + indicatif
notes.body: The single most common B2 slip in a debate. « Bien que ce soit un héritage » — subjunctive. « Même si c’est un héritage » — indicative. Quoique behaves like bien que; the false friend quoi que (two words) means whatever and is something else entirely. The three survival forms after bien que are soit, ait and puisse.

notes.title: La Réunion — quatre religions, un seul calendrier
notes.body: Catholics, Tamil Hindus, Muslims and a Chinese community have shared the island since the nineteenth century, and Dipavali, l’Aïd, Noël and the Chinese New Year are all publicly marked. Interfaith marriage is ordinary rather than remarkable. In an exam, stay abstract — le vivre-ensemble, le métissage, la diversité religieuse. The Creole words « malbar » and « zarabe » belong to insiders: recognise them, don’t use them.

notes.title: Quasquara — l’affaire en trois dates
notes.body: In 2022 the commune of Quasquara, in Corse-du-Sud, put up a cross at the entrance to the village. A resident asked for its removal, the mayor refused, and in 2025 the tribunal administratif de Bastia annulled that refusal. On 26 June 2026 the cour administrative d’appel de Marseille confirmed it: a cross erected in 2022, at a different spot from an older one, is a new religious sign and not the replacement of a pre-1905 cross.

notes.title: « Porter plainte » is not the right verb here
notes.body: The press writes « après la plainte d’une habitante », and in everyday French that passes — but it is loose. Une plainte is criminal: you porter plainte against a person, at the police or the procureur. A cross on communal land is an administrative matter, so what you actually do is demander le retrait, then déposer un recours against the mayor’s refusal. Using the right one in an exam is a visible mark of register.

examples: À La Réunion, quatre religions cohabitent dans le même village. (ko-a-BEET)
Les mariages mixtes y sont ordinaires depuis des générations. (lay ma-RYAZH MEEKST)
En Corse, la croix est autant un symbole identitaire qu’un symbole religieux. (sam-BOL ee-dahn-tee-TEHR)
La commune a érigé une croix à l’entrée du village en 2022. (a ay-ree-ZHAY ewn KRWAH)
Une habitante a déposé un recours devant le tribunal administratif. (day-po-ZAY uhn ruh-KOOR)
Bien que la croix soit un héritage local, le tribunal a ordonné son retrait. (byan kuh lah krwah SWAH)
practice: Bien que or même si? — « ___ la croix soit ancienne, elle date de 2022. » · « ___ la croix est ancienne, la loi s’applique. »
Contrast the two islands in four sentences, using alors que · contrairement à · en revanche · pourtant.
Tell the Quasquara story in six sentences, in the past, with the verbs from the second table.
Porter plainte or déposer un recours? — a stolen bike · a cross on communal land · a noisy neighbour · a refused building permit.
Answer out loud in two minutes: « Une croix peut-elle être culturelle plutôt que religieuse ? »
Now say what the two islands have in common — not only what separates them.
tutorPrompt: Act as a DELF B2 examiner, in French throughout. The topic is two French islands: La Réunion, where Catholics, Tamil Hindus, Muslims and a Chinese community share the same calendar and interfaith marriage is ordinary, and la Corse, where a largely Catholic identity met the loi de 1905 in the affaire de la croix de Quasquara — a cross erected by the commune in 2022, a resident’s demande de retrait, the mayor’s refusal annulled by the tribunal administratif de Bastia in 2025, and the removal confirmed by the cour administrative d’appel de Marseille on 26 June 2026. Make me compare the two islands out loud, then defend a position on whether a cross can be « culturelle plutôt que religieuse ». Correct exactly two things per turn: the opposition connectors — alors que and même si take the indicative, bien que and quoique take the subjunctive, contrairement à takes a noun — and my choice between porter plainte and déposer un recours. Finish with three concrete fixes and the phrases I hesitated on.

title: L'eau & le chlordécone — la Guadeloupe au concret
goal: Two documented cases that turn a vague argument about inequality into a good one — and the connectors of cause and consequence you need to lay them out.

figures.alt: Two panels on Guadeloupe. On the left, the water network: of every 100 litres produced, roughly 70 are lost to leaks and only about 30 reach a tap; les tours d'eau cover about 20 percent of the territory but affect resources serving more than half the population; the SMGEAG has run water for the island since 2021 and aims to repair 5 000 leaks by the end of 2026. On the right, a timeline of le chlordécone, the pesticide used on banana plantations: spread from 1972, banned in mainland France in 1990, but allowed in the Antilles under a derogation until 1993 — three years highlighted as the heart of the argument. In 2021 prostate cancer linked to it was recognised as an occupational disease; in 2023 the criminal case ended in a non-lieu.
figures.caption: The two amber bars are the argument. On the left, most of the water never reaches a tap. On the right, three years in which a pesticide banned in the Hexagone stayed legal here — which is why this file comes up every time someone asks whether the rules are the same everywhere.

vocab.en: a dismissal — the case never reaches trial

grammar.point: Cause and consequence — and the one choice English never makes you make

table.title: dire pourquoi, et dire ce qui en résulte

rows.label: une cause — phrase
cells: parce que le réseau est vétuste

table.note: English says « because of » for good news and bad alike. French makes you take a side: à cause de blames, grâce à credits. « Grâce aux fuites » would be sarcasm, and « à cause du nouveau plan » would be an accusation — so pick deliberately, and use en raison de when you want to stay neutral.

table2.title: Le chlordécone — l’affaire en cinq dates

le produit est interdit en France

grammar.explain: To argue a case rather than just deplore it, you need the words that link a cause to its effect — and French sorts them by what follows and by whose side you are on. À cause de, grâce à, en raison de and faute de all take a noun, never a clause, so you say à cause des fuites and not « à cause que ». Parce que and car take a full clause. On the consequence side, donc, c'est pourquoi and par conséquent simply introduce the result. The choice that catches English speakers is the first pair: « because of » is neutral in English, while à cause de assigns blame and grâce à gives credit. Saying « grâce à la pollution » is not a small slip — it reads as sarcasm. When you genuinely want neutrality, en raison de is the word, and it is also the one you will meet in any official report.

notes.title: À cause de blames, grâce à credits
notes.body: Both are « because of », and French will not let you sit on the fence. À cause des coupures, the shortage is someone's fault; grâce au nouveau plan, someone gets the credit. Backwards, you sound sarcastic rather than wrong — worse in an oral. En raison de is the neutral third option, and the one official reports use. All three take a noun: never « à cause que ».

notes.title: L'eau — pourquoi elle n'arrive pas
notes.body: The problem is not rainfall, it is the pipes. Around seventy per cent of the water produced leaks away before reaching a tap, so whole areas live on des tours d'eau — a rota where the supply is cut for a day or more. They cover about a fifth of the territory but touch more than half the population. Since 2021 le SMGEAG has run the network.

notes.title: Le chlordécone — les trois ans qui font tout l'argument
notes.body: A pesticide used on banana plantations from 1972, banned in mainland France in 1990 — and kept legal in Guadeloupe and Martinique by ministerial derogation until 1993. It stays in the soil for centuries, and more than ninety per cent of adults on both islands carry it in their blood. In 2021 the ANSES found a probable causal link with prostate cancer and a decree made that cancer an occupational disease.

notes.title: 2009 — les quarante-quatre jours du LKP
notes.body: Both files feed one grievance: la vie chère. On 20 January 2009 le LKP — Liyannaj Kont Pwofitasyon, Creole for « alliance against profiteering » — a collective of some fifty organisations led by Élie Domota, brought Guadeloupe to a standstill for forty-four days, and the movement spread to Martinique, la Guyane and La Réunion. It ended on 4 March with a 165-article agreement and a 200-euro rise on the lowest wages.

notes.title: Un non-lieu is not an acquittal
notes.body: The criminal case, opened on a 2006 complaint, ended in January 2023 in un non-lieu: the investigating judges found insufficient grounds to send anyone to trial. That is not une relaxe, which is an acquittal after a trial, and not a finding that nothing happened. Separately, an administrative court has recognised the State's « négligences fautives ».
